events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description:
The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.
Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.
The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.
Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.
Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.
Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | De y para el pueblo / By and for the People: Revolutionary Mexican Prints
events.description: The exhibit features highlights from The Bancroft Library's extensive collection of prints. The show examines how a Mexico City-based artists collective, the Taller de Gráfica Popular (Workshop for Popular Graphic Art), built an artistic legacy, tracing its roots from José Guadalupe Posada's portrayals of everyday Mexican life, to its enduring influence on artists on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border today.

events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Bernice Layne Brown Gallery (inside Doe Library)
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description:
At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.
The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. Mounted archival digital print, 36 x 48 inches each. Titles and dates as published in Remembering the Future. Courtesy of the artist.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Exhibition Team:Lauren Graves, Guest CuratorAlissa Schapiro and Hannah Weisman, Coordinating CuratorsAndrea Calderon, RegistrarDavid Sullivan, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Special thanks to Michael S. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.
Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Film Screening: Modern Times
events.description: It starts with an overhead shot of sheep and cuts to the throngs coming out of a subway station. Was Charlie Chaplin a Surrealist, or just a realist? His version of modern times looks forward in equal measure to Jacques Tati and 1984. This "silent" is full of modern sounds, heard over loudspeakers and big corporate television screens (not to mention the Tramp's outburst of French-inspired gibberish). Charlie, the ever-elegant Tramp, is an industrial swashbuckler with an oilcan for a sword, but he's begun taking on the characteristics of factory machines, obsessively twisting buttons no matter where they are.

events.title: Film Screening: The Last Waltz
events.description: Martin Scorsese grew up listening to seminal rock DJ Alan Freed, and from Mean Streets onward, his movies have been driven by the power of rock and roll. His love of music is innate and instinctual, so when The Band decided to hang it up after seventeen years on the road, they chose Scorsese to film their farewell concert at Winterland Ballroom on Thanksgiving 1976. The film intercuts the glorious music from one of the all-time great concert lineups with interviews with members of The Band as they talk about their lives and music. The Last Waltz is an elegiac masterpiece that captures a special moment in music history.

events.title: Film Screening: Center Stage
events.description: After a string of memorable performances as strong-willed, beautiful, and virtuous women, the actress Ruan Lingyu committed suicide in 1935, at the age of twenty-four. Stanley Kwan's innovative film goes far beyond the traditional biopic to offer up several strata of "reality," "reenactment," and "cinema." Detailed re-creations of scenes from the actress's too-short life combine with documentary interviews of her contemporaries, actual footage from her existing silent films, and even discussions between star Maggie Cheung, Kwan, and other cast members. Like a Russian doll, Center Stage reveals a Modernist take on the ways in which cinema and culture create an actress, a legend, and a woman.

events.description: "What is acting after all?" Maddalena (Anna Magnani) rhetorically asks before the mirror in Luchino Visconti's melodrama of mother love and misplaced ambition. Magnani's extraordinary performance is its own answer. As a working-class mother desperate to get her young daughter a shot at stardom through a Cinecittà casting call, Magnani turns what might have been a simplistic caricature of a domineering stage mother into a fully rendered character, both hilarious and tragically human. Visconti's direction similarly refuses to distinguish between satire and sincerity; even while it mocks the business of moviemaking, Bellissima is an exquisite example of the filmmaker's craft.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description:
On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.
Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.description: This adaptation of Fyodor Dostoyevsky's tale about displaced, disconnected people drifting along crossing, doubling paths was shot in moody black-and-white on a soundstage simulacrum of Livorno, Italy. With it Luchino Visconti veered away from verisimilitude and toward an emphatically subjective style—from neorealism to neoromanticism. As a quiet man who accidentally befriends a troubled, lonely young woman (Maria Schell) and finds himself playing understudy for the absent object of her affections (Jean Marais), Marcello Mastroianni mingles subtly passionate yearnings with a characteristic note of annoyance. His character is both distrustful of and seduced by the romantic dreams that preoccupy the woman he loves.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: The hyperinvariant subspace problem
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Hari Bercovici, Indiana University at BloomingtonAmong the results announced by Open AI, there is a solution of the hyperinvariant subspace problem: there is an operator T on a Hilbert space that is not a scalar multiple of the identity, does have nontrivial invariant subspaces, but none of these subspaces is invariant under every operator in the commutant of T. In particular, the commutant (T)' is a nonselfadjoint transitive algebra. The construction uses weighted shifts with few invariant subspaces, and a modicum of ergodic theory: a transformation known as an odometer. The resulting operator T is quasinilpotent. I will argue that the example is correct. Moreover, the example can be modified so that it yields a contraction with essential spectrum equal to the closed unit disk. Such contractions are known to have a large variety of invariant subspaces, and one could ask whether the techniques used to produce these subspaces can be improved to yield a hyperinvariant subspace.

events.title: Adaptive Traffic Control Systems
events.description: Description This newly updated online course offers a summary of fundamental principles, operational requirements and expected benefits of some of the frequently deployed Adaptive Traffic Control Systems. The first session presents various traffic control systems and general characteristics, market state, and evaluations of the ATCS along with other solutions like traffic responsive and Artificial Intelligent (AI) based signal timing. The second session focuses on SCATS (one of the oldest and widely deployed systems in the entire world) and other ATCSs from the US market. The third session presents SynchroGreen and InSync, recent ATCSs which recently gained a lot of popularity among the US customers. Finally, the fourth session addresses SCOOT and ACS Lite, two systems with similarities in algorithms but various detection and communication requirements. Each session is divided into three major parts: the first offers a summary of fundamental principles of a selected adaptive technology, the second covers summary of operational and institutional requirements to run adaptive control, and the third presents operational benefits from available case studies. Topics IncludeFundamental principles of ATCS operations Adjustment of signal timings and operational flexibility Traffic responsive and AI based signal timing Detection requirements Communication requirements Software and hardware requirements Reported operational modes Institutional preparation for deployment of an ATCS Reported operational benefits What You Will Learn Students will obtain a significant amount of technical information to understand fundamental principles of operations, deployment requirements, and reported operational benefits (highlighted through exemplary case studies) of some of the frequently deployed Adaptive Traffic Control Systems. This information will help students to become familiar with these relatively new signal control technologies and develop a realistic set of expectations regarding their deployments and operational benefits. Who Should Attend This course is intended for traffic engineers, planners, technicians, and decision makers in municipal, county, and state agencies interested in the operations, requirements and benefits of Adaptive Traffic Control System technologies, particularly those with the responsibility for the planning, design, implementation, operation, and maintenance of traffic signal control systems for urban areas.

events.title: TAC Seminar - Simona Miller (LIGO)
events.description:
Title: Measuring Black Hole Spin with Gravitational Waves: From Single Events to the Astrophysical PopulationAbstract: Over the past decade, the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) detector network has recorded hundreds of gravitational-wave signals from binary black hole mergers. Gravitational waves remain the sole means to directly measure a black hole's spin, or intrinsic angular momentum—a property that serves as a unique probe of astrophysical processes ranging from sub-stellar to cosmological scales. Yet black hole spin remains poorly constrained: it has a comparatively weak imprint on gravitational-wave signals, can mimic other physical effects, and is highly susceptible to features in detector noise and systematic modelling uncertainty. Without careful safeguards, we risk spurious spin inference and false astrophysical conclusions. I will describe efforts to produce accurate, precise, and unbiased black hole spin inference at every stage of LVK data analysis, from exceptional events such as the two most-massive binary black hole mergers observed to date, to the population writ large following the recent GWTC-5 data release.

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Joseph Checkelsky: Natural Superlattice Materials and Modulated Superconductivity
events.description: Natural Superlattice Materials and Modulated Superconductivity Abstract: Connecting theoretical models for exotic quantum states to real materials is a key goal in quantum materials synthesis. Two-dimensional model systems have been proposed to host a wide variety of exotic phases- historically a number of techniques have been used to realize these including thin film growth and mechanical exfoliation. We describe here our recent progress in experimentally realizing 2D model systems using bulk crystal synthesis including modulated superconducting states. We discuss their structures and the new phenomena that they support. We comment on the perspective for realizing further 2D model systems in complex material structures and their connections to other methods for realizing 2D systems.

events.title: Seminar 271, Development: Jonathan Weigel and Anja Benshaul-Tolonen
Aashish Manglik: "Improvising on a Fold: From Odorants to Opioids"
events.description: The seven-transmembrane fold is among evolution's most heavily reused solutions to molecular detection, elaborated in humans into roughly 800 receptors that transduce stimuli from single photons and protons to peptide hormones and much of the sensible volatile chemical space. Yet we still cannot specify from sequence alone what a receptor detects, or how strongly a ligand will activate it. I will describe how deep mutational scanning, paired with structural interrogation, resolves this mapping in two systems at opposite extremes of ligand promiscuity: odorant receptors, where broad chemical tuning appears purchased at the expense of folding stability, and the opioid receptors, where saturating mutagenesis exposes the determinants of agonist efficacy. Together they begin to define how evolution repurposes a single fold to meet new demands.

events.title: Aashish Manglik: Structural & Quantitative Biology Seminar
Physics Colloquium with Eoin Brodie: Coarse-Graining Microbial Life: From Genomes to Ecosystem Fluxes
events.description: Coarse-Graining Microbial Life: From Genomes to Ecosystem Fluxes Abstract: Microbes transform the chemistry of our planet, yet their extraordinary diversity makes their collective behavior difficult to predict. How much biological detail must we retain to connect genomes to ecosystem function? I will explore how energy budgets, biophysical constraints, and trade-offs can reduce genomic complexity to a tractable set of microbial traits. Using examples from plant–microbe interactions and methane emissions along a permafrost thaw gradient, I will show how these traits connect cellular resource use to ecosystem carbon fluxes. I will close with the challenge of predicting how microbial communities, and their effects on the environment, emerge across scales.

events.title: "Behind Bars: How Votive Objects Mediated Liberation and Enslavement at Conques" by Kris N. Racaniello
events.description:
"Behind Bars: How Votive Objects Mediated Liberation and Enslavement at Conques" by Kris N. RacanielloAbstract: A burdensome metal, associated with implements of war and captivity, iron acquired a striking duality within medieval shrines: it represented bodies imprisoned and bound by its wicked weight but also made free and even sometimes converted from Islam to Christianity. This talk examines the surviving Romanesque wrought ironwork in the Abbey Church of Sainte Foy at Conques, alongside vanished votive objects documented in its miracle collection (the Liber miraculorum sancte Fidis). As we will see, these grilles made of votive iron came to function as a protective interface, enveloping the golden Majesty of Sainte Foy in a curling thicket of iron, overlaying material metaphors that fundamentally altered the reliquary's reception. This research demonstrates that votive shackles had several conflicting functions in shrines. They offered Christian viewers tangible hope for liberation from oppression, but their presence also amplifyed the spiritual authority and attractive persona at the core of the site. This work reveals an additional narrative underlying many stories of liberation: namely, Muslim people are described as wicked captors, rightfully subjugated by Latin Christians. Notably absent, however, from these narratives are the historically enslaved persons who worked the monastic lands of Conques. By recovering votive objects and reading metalwork alongside texts, we can trace these archivally voiceless lives and uncover the processes of race-making and enslavement active in Romanesque Conques. Centering iron, an overlooked material, reveals the shrine as a richly layered narrative space and a vital physical record sustaining new histories of race, personhood, and righteous territorial expansion.
Bio: Dr. Kris Racaniello is a historian of medieval art whose work explores how sacred objects and spaces construct power, memory, identity, and territory. Currently an Adjunct Professor of the History of Art at the Fashion Institute of Technology and Purchase College, SUNY, they earned their PhD from the CUNY Graduate Center in 2026. Their research examines Romanesque shrine complexes built between 1099 and 1144. Racaniello argues that objects were strategically arranged around reliquaries to materialize rhetoric, allowing religious communities to reinvent their histories and assert territorial claims. This work was vitally supported by a Kress Fellowship at the Bibliotheca Hertziana–Max Planck Institute for Art History in Rome. Racaniello's research appears in several journals and edited volumes, including Different Visions, Convivium, Mediaevalia, and Public Art Dialogue. They are also a co-author of the 2025 monograph Conques Across Time: Inventions and Reinventions (9th to 21st Centuries), which represents the culmination of their contributions to a four-year international research project.

events.title: Sunrise Lecture by Lea Pao: "The Poetics of Information Aesthetics: Bense Reading Mayröcker"
events.description: This talk sketches the micro- and macroscopic details of the little-known encounter between German philosopher and cybernetician Max Bense and Austrian poet Friederike Mayröcker in the 1960s. Bense, operating at the intersection of postwar literary culture, cybernetics, and information theory, was both an early pioneer of computer art and aesthetics and a key figure in the experimental poetry scene. He published and edited multiple literary journals, invited poets and artists to Stuttgart, and fostered collaborations and relationships across international networks. This openness towards avant-garde experiments led Mayröcker to send Bense a manuscript of her poetry for his magazine edition rot. Her first independent collection Larifari in 1956 received lukewarm reception in Austria, where it was deemed "confusing" and "immature"; in Bense, Mayröcker found an advocate for poetics risks and unestablished poets. The talk offers an anatomy of Bense as a reader of Mayröcker. Through archival materials, personal correspondence, and publication histories, I trace Bense's conceptual thinking about information aesthetics and semiotics via his understanding of Mayröcker's linguistic and poetic experiments. Bense's reading of Mayröcker reveals the centrality of poetic practice to his theory of text and the material, combinatory understanding of textuality at the core of his information aesthetics. Lea Pao is Associate Professor of German Studies and Director of German Studies at Stanford University. Her research interests include German and Austrian poetry, the history of information and its theories, and literary theory. Her book An Archaeology of Forgotten Information Practices (Cornell UP, 2026) explores the ways in which ideas about information—and the history of twentieth-century information theory—can shape our thinking about poetry's social, cultural, and linguistic work, and vice versa.

events.title: Fall 2026 Senior Thesis Exhibition: "Windows to Here"
events.location: Worth Ryder Art Gallery, Anthropology and Art Building, Rm 116. Near the intersection of College Ave. & Bancroft Way
events.description:
Worth Ryder Art Gallery and the Department of Art Practice are excited to announce Windows to Here, the Department of Art Practice's Fall 2026 Senior Thesis Exhibition featuring multidisciplinary artworks by seventeen Art Practice majors. Fog covers and clears over a distant view of the Golden Gate Bridge. A jogger runs by, pulled by his dog. A family sits down to dinner. A cat curls up on a sill. A dog peers out expectantly. A professor lectures to a room full of students. A friend walks by on their way to class. Rain pours down and I reach to close my window. Are artworks windows into artists' understandings of the world? The Fall 2026 Senior Thesis Exhibition Windows to Here frames seventeen different artists' views of spaces, experiences, aspirations and imaginaries through the mediums of painting, sculpture, printmaking and installation. These student artists gaze inward toward personal identity, childhood, and inherited histories, and they look outward toward cultural belonging, migration, labor, and the environments we live in. Rather than offering a single perspective, Windows to Here invites viewers to encounter the many ways we see and experience the world we share. What do you see through the window?
Windows to Here features artworks by students in Brody Reiman and Anne Walsh's ART185 Senior Projects/Professional Practices classes, supported by Graduate Student Instructor Lorain Khalil Rihan.

events.title: Applied Math Seminar: A priori error analysis for the Shliomis ferrofluid model without magnetic regularization
events.description: Speaker: Gonzalo Benavides, University of MarylandWe develop and analyze a family of conforming, energy-stable spatial semidiscretizations of the Shliomis ferrofluid model in two and three space dimensions. Unlike many existing numerical analyses, we treat the system without introducing magnetic diffusion. The limited spatial control supplied by the energy law complicates the treatment of magnetic nonlinearities in the error analysis. Our formulation retains the rotational coupling and nonlinear magnetic relaxation and incorporates the magnetic normal-flux condition naturally, overcoming the dimensional restriction and boundary-enforcement difficulties of the two-potential approach of Benavides, Nochetto and Shakipov (2026). The error analysis combines consistent stabilization of the Maxwell constraint with a cancellation arising from exact incompressibility and the pointwise symmetry of the Hessian of the magnetic potential. We prove global solvability of the semidiscrete scheme and establish a priori error estimates for sufficiently regular exact solutions under explicit approximation and projection-stability assumptions. We also construct an averaged $H^2$-conforming projector, following Girault and Scott (2002), that is defined on $L^1$, and establish its Sobolev approximation and stability properties. These properties are needed for the error analysis and are of independent interest.

events.description:
Amy Weeks, Assistant Professor, University of Wisconsin, MadisonNew enzyme chemistry to decipher post-translational modification function Spatial organization and temporal dynamics are essential properties of cellular signaling. Post-translational modifications (PTMs) to proteins relay biological signals by exerting precise spatiotemporal control over protein function, localization, and lifetime. A systems-level experimental map of post-translationally modified proteins across subcellular space and time would transform our understanding of how PTMs orchestrate complex cellular functions in response to biological stimuli. However, such a map is inaccessible with current technologies. To meet this challenge, the Weeks lab is focused on developing new chemical and enzymatic tools for PTM proteomics with subcellular spatial and temporal resolution. We develop chemical probes and genetically targetable, PTM-selective proximity labeling enzymes to covalently tag post-translationally modified proteins in specific subcellular locations, enabling their enrichment and analysis with mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiments. We focus on two pervasive PTMs, proteolysis and phosphorylation, both of which play critical roles in myriad biological signaling pathways relevant to human health and disease. Our technologies are broadly applicable to a wide variety of protease and kinase signaling pathways and provide an integrated view of cellular signaling with implications for both fundamental biological discovery and therapeutic innovation.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Importing Aggregate Demand"
events.description: Abstract: How exposed are open economies to global demand shocks? In equilibrium, foreign booms can be absorbed either by domestic consumption ("quantities") or by real exchange rate appreciation ("prices"). We show that failures of Ricardian equivalence and global financial market imperfections, two frictions popular in much recent work, have opposite effects on the split: while elevated marginal propensities to consume push towards quantities, financial frictions instead increase price adjustment. As the flexible-price equilibrium generally features a mix of quantity and price responses, policy needs to be contractionary to achieve flexible-price outcomes if the spending effect dominates, and vice-versa if financial frictions are severe. In our quantitative explorations the spending effect tends to win the race, necessitating aggressive domestic policy action.

events.title: Seminar 221 Industrial Organization: Ashvin Gandhi – Misinformation and Mistrust in the Marketplace: Evidence from Online Ratings Manipulation
events.description: Abstract: Fake product reviews—and the manipulation of reputation systems by sellers more broadly—are a widespread issue for two-sided platforms. We study two primary channels through which such manipulation can affect market outcomes: (i) creating misinformation about the reviewed product, and (ii) breeding mistrust in the ratings system overall. To examine these in the Amazon.com marketplace, we measure misinformation by observing products purchasing fake reviews and measure mistrust by eliciting shoppers' beliefs about the prevalence of fake reviews on Amazon through an incentivized survey experiment. We incorporate these into a structural model of demand in which consumers form beliefs about product quality based on observed reviews and perceptions about their trustworthiness. Counterfactual policy simulations indicate that fake reviews reduce consumer welfare, shift sales from honest to dishonest sellers, and ultimately harm the platform. Welfare losses arise primarily from misinformation that leads to worse purchases. While mistrust also leads to purchasing mistakes, its consumer welfare effects are largely dominated by increased price competition under a weakened ratings system. Finally, we identify key limitations in platforms' incentives to police manipulation and evaluate enforcement alternatives.

events.title: Beyond the Skinner Box of AI Competence: Modeling Professional Judgment for AI-Mediated Teaching and Learning
events.location: 4215 - Berkeley Way West, and via Zoom
events.description: As generative artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes teaching, learning, assessment, and professional practice, teacher education faces increasing pressure to prepare candidates for AI-mediated educational environments. Much of the emerging discourse has focused on developing AI competencies, technical skills, or AI literacy frameworks for teachers (OECD, 2025). Comparatively little attention has been given to the professional learning of teacher educators themselves or to the forms of professional judgment required to design meaningful learning experiences in which AI becomes a productive educational partner rather than a substitute for human expertise. This presentation argues that AI literacy is fundamentally a problem of evolving professional judgment rather than technological proficiency. Drawing on grounded theory analyses of sixty interviews with teacher educators, preservice teachers, and practicing educators, we examine how instructors are reconceptualizing curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, and ethical decision making in response to rapidly changing AI capabilities. From these analyses we introduce the Five Pillars of Practice—Accuracy, Agency, Accessibility, Assessment, and Authenticity—as a learning-centered framework (Duckor & Holmberg, 2026) that organizes recurring dilemmas encountered in teacher education while providing a coherent architecture for faculty development and program redesign. Rather than functioning as a competency checklist, the Five Pillars describe domains in which teacher educators continually exercise, refine, and make visible professional judgments about learning, evidence, human agency, and responsible AI use. The framework positions AI literacy constructs developmentally, as an emergent capacity that develops through disciplined instructional and assessment for deeper learning decision making, rather than mastery of particular technologies. The seminar presentation concludes by considering implications for teacher education curriculum, faculty professional learning, program assessment, and the preparation of future educators capable of designing AI-mediated learning environments that preserve ambitious teaching, deeper learning, and human development. Reconceptualizing AI literacy as professional judgment provides a constructively aligned foundation for preparing teachers whose expertise remains adaptive as AI technologies continue to evolve in the current paradigm shift (Kuhn, 1962).

events.title: OpenADMET (Bay Area Open Science Group)
events.description:
OpenADMET - Raising the bar on ADMET prediction with open sciencevZoom information registrationDrug discovery programs frequently stall due to the Avoid-ome, which comprises the complex off-target interactions and ADMET liabilities that traditional heuristic methods struggle to address. To solve this, OpenADMET combines high-resolution structural biology, directed data generation, and machine learning into a systematic framework for predicting and mitigating these liabilities. Central to this mission is generating targeted datasets to host large-scale blind benchmarks that test community predictive models on real-world drug design problems. By uniting hundreds of academic and industry teams through these challenges, webinars, and conferences, the initiative fosters widespread collaboration to establish transparent, data-driven standards across the field.
Pat Walters is Chief Scientist at OpenADMET, an open-science initiative that integrates high-throughput experimentation, structural biology, and machine learning to advance ADMET prediction. Alongside his work at OpenADMET, he serves as an Adjunct Professor in the Department of Bioengineering & Therapeutic Sciences at UCSF. Pat brings over thirty years of industry leadership to his roles, having previously held senior positions at Relay Therapeutics and Vertex Pharmaceuticals. A dedicated educator and communicator, he is the author of the widely read blog "Practical Cheminformatics," where he shares technical insights on computational drug discovery.
Bay Area Open Science GroupThe Bay Area Open Science Group is a growing community for Bay Area academics and researchers interested in incorporating open science into their research, teaching, and learning. Targeting students, faculty, and staff at UCSF, Berkeley, and Stanford, the goal of the community is to increase awareness of and engagement with all things open science, including open access articles, open research data, open source software, and open educational resources. Through this work the group hopes to connect researchers with tools they can use to make the products and process of science more equitable and reproducible.

Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics: David Huffman "Minds, Models and Markets: How Managerial Cognition Affects Pricing Strategies"
events.description: Abstract: We investigate how bounded rationality of firm managers affects pricing strategies using data from a firm with over 20,000 gas station managers. Managers with lower cognitive skills exhibit systematically different mental models of optimal price, favoring lower prices, and this persists in the face of experience. This partly reflects not anticipating how competitors respond to price cuts. Consequences include more price wars, lower profits and producer surplus, but higher consumer surplus and market efficiency. Our findings demonstrate that cognitive constraints can systematically affect repeated price competitions, with important theoretical, welfare, and policy implications Paper Link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1IwwuRWOfJTR_34OcQaJKtWMRr5JEH-kO/view?usp=sharing

events.title: Local and Global: PCPs Meet High-Dimensional Expanders | Richard M. Karp Distinguished Lecture
Aaron Nyerges, "Counter-Mapping Modernism: Literature, Oil, and the Cartographic Imagination"
events.description:
Aaron Nyerges' recent book American Modernism and the Cartographic Imagination (Cambridge UP, 2025) is a new reading of American modernism that examines the cartographic literature of the United States and places it in context of the state's overseas expansion. Dr Nyerges stretches the map of US literature across an imperial archipelago of territories and outlines a method of comparative reading that brings canonical American authors into dialogue with under-represented writers from across the contested dominions of US empire. He argues that literary artists from across US dominion responded to space-dominating technologies of empire and retooled them to imagine counter-cartographies, designs that challenged the official geographies of the United States. This talk explores the cartographic imagination of modernist literature as it relates to the territorial expansions of the United States in the early decades of the twentieth century. We begin with Langston Hughes's construction and destruction of cartographic material, his tearing apart of his world atlas, and his vision of a nation made errant by oceanic flux. From there we will assemble – and collaboratively analyse – a group of poems that make visible the divergent investments modernists made in the production of "counter-maps," forms of geographic knowledge that challenge the maps made by governments and corporations. In particular, we will attend to the oil maps deposited in Ezra Pound's Cantos, by which he critiques the resource expropriation of former Ottoman territories by Anglo-American cartels. At that very locus, the Iraqi modernist poet Nazik al-Malā'ikah envisions a different kind of energy poetics, where the dividing line between oil's extractive and consumptive spheres is decidedly smudged. Her mapping of an abysmal geography provides anti-colonial counterpoint to the expanding highway infrastructure of the United States, as well as the thermodynamic aesthetics that exhilarate the lyrics of Pound and William Carlos Williams.
Aaron Nyerges (https://www.ussc.edu.au/aaron-nyerges) is a Senior Lecturer in American Studies at the United States Studies Centre, University of Sydney. His book, American Modernism and the Cartographic Imagination, was published by Cambridge University Press in 2025.

events.title: Book Talk: An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa
events.description: Book Talk:An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa (Cambridge University Press, 2026) In what measure could education be an agent of African freedom? Combining histories of race, economics, and education, Elisa Prosperetti examines this question in two West African contexts, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, from the 1890s to the 1980s. She argues that a Black Atlantic perspective changes how we see decolonization and development in West Africa, by revealing schooling's essential role in aspirations of African emancipation. Rejecting colonial exploitation of the African body, proponents of anticolonial development instead claimed the mind as the site of economic productivity for African people. An Anticolonial Development shows how, in the middle of the twentieth century, Africans proposed an original understanding of development that fused antiracism to economic theory, and human dignity to material productivity. Elisa Prosperetti is an Assistant Professor of History at the National Institute of Education/Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. She is a historian of modern African and global history, specializing in histories of race, development, education, and decolonization, with a geographic focus on West Africa and the Black Atlantic world. She received her PhD in History from Princeton University in 2020, and currently serves on the Editorial Review Board of the African Studies Review and as a podcast host for the African Studies channel of the New Books Network.

events.description: Angela Gronenborn, UPMC Rosalind Franklin Professor, University of PittsburghThe awesome power of fluorine NMR - from drugs to cells Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a versatile tool for probing structure, dynamics, folding, and interactions at atomic resolution. While naturally occurring magnetically active isotopes, such as 1H, 13C, or 15N, are most commonly used in biomolecular NMR, with 15N and 13C isotopic labeling routinely employed at the present time, 19F is a very attractive and sensitive alternative nucleus, which offers rich information on the structure and dynamics of molecules. This presentation will summarize the unique benefits of 19F NMR spectroscopy for the study of biomolecular systems. Particular focus will be placed on the most recent studies and on unique and important potential applications of fluorine NMR methodology.

events.title: Film Screening | My Father and Qaddafi
events.description:
My Father and Qaddafi Film Screening and Director Q&ADate and time of event: Tuesday, December 1, 5:00 PMEvent location: Richard & Rhoda Goldman Theater • David Brower Center • 2150 Allston Way, Suite 100 • BerkeleyThe Center for Middle Eastern Studies presents a film screening of My Father and Qaddafi, followed by a Q&A with director Jihan. Film Summary: When Jihan was six years old, her father flew to Cairo and never returned. Mansur Rashid Kikhia was the Foreign Minister of Libya, ambassador to the United Nations, and a human rights lawyer. After serving in Qaddafi's increasingly brutal regime, he defected from the government and became the leader of the peaceful opposition. For many, Kikhia was a rising star who could have been the next leader of Libya, however, in 1993 he disappeared from his hotel in Egypt. Jihan's mother Baha Al Omary, a strong-willed Syrian-American artist, began searching for him, launching the family into an international political maze. Her mission to find justice brought her to the Libyan desert in the middle of the night, face to face with Qaddafi to negotiate her husband's release. Yet it wasn't until after the regime's fall, 19 years later, that his body was found in a freezer near Qaddafi's palace.
My Father and Qaddafi takes the audience on a raw and reflective journey as Jihan pieces together a father she barely remembers, while discovering the troubled history and politics of Libya. Her journey starts from fading personal memories, leading to encounters with family members, her father's peers, and historical archive footage. Hoping at first to uncover the truth, Jihan instead transforms the mystery into a curiosity that brings her closer to her father and her Libyan identity. She approaches politics not as a distant subject, but as a lived experience that penetrates into every human relationship - even between a little girl and her father. Gil (https://www.towson.edu/cla/departments/socioanthrocrim/facultystaff/hgill.html)l, Professor of Anthropology at Towson University and an award-winning documentary filmmaker, based on his new book, Coming of Age in Macholand: Masculinity, Patriarchy, and the Search for Freedom in Indian Punjab (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand) (University of Chicago Press, forthcoming in Nov 2026), an eye-opening examination of masculinity, violence, and transnational migration focused on present-day Indian Punjab. Pre-order the book now. Only limited copies will be available to purchase at the event" - https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand). Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ———–DATE: Tue, Dec 1, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKIn Coming of Age in Macholand (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand), anthropologist and filmmaker Harjant Gill examines how Punjabi men in India, disillusioned by promises of power and control, contend with patriarchy: by submitting to it, attempting to transgress it, migrating to escape it, or coming undone by it. Gill takes readers deep inside men's worlds to show how boys come of age and how masculinity is produced through pervasive violence, while also being underwritten by intimacy, fraternal love, and homosocial bonds. Based on four years of fieldwork conducted over a decade and hundreds of interviews, Gill explores how boys learn to become men against the backdrop of patriarchal constraints, political violence, shifting agrarian economies, and steady outward migration. He shows the extent to which violence is a function and a reflection of powerlessness. By tracing the making of masculinity in a society where sexuality is sanctioned almost exclusively through heteronormative frameworks of marriage and family, this book documents how patriarchy forecloses agency and autonomy. Ultimately, Coming of Age in Macholand offers a powerful indictment of patriarchy as a system that not only oppresses women and queer people, but also constricts men's intimate, sexual, and emotional lives. ABOUT THE AUTHORHarjant Gill (https://www.towson.edu/cla/departments/socioanthrocrim/facultystaff/hgill.html) is a professor of anthropology and an award-winning documentary filmmaker whose work bridges ethnography, visual storytelling, and public scholarship. His research and creative practice explore masculinity, migration, media, religion, and popular culture in South Asia and its diasporas, with a particular focus on Punjab and Sikh communities. Through film and writing, he examines how intimate lives are shaped by patriarchy, nationalism, violence, and transnational mobility. Gill is the director of the internationally recognized documentary films Roots of Love, Mardistan/Macholand, and Sent Away Boys. His work has been broadcast on the BBC, PBS, and Doordarshan and screened widely at universities, film festivals, and public forums around the world. His scholarship appears in leading journals including American Anthropologist, Ethnography, and Visual Anthropology Review. His forthcoming book, Coming of Age in Macholand (University of Chicago Press), offers a deeply personal ethnographic exploration of patriarchy, masculinity, violence, and migration in Indian Punjab. Gill has received fellowships and awards from the American Institute of Indian Studies, Fulbright-Nehru, Point Foundation, Wenner-Gren, Whiting, and Woodrow Wilson foundations. Born in Chandigarh (India), Gill grew up in SF Bay Area and now lives in Washington, DC. EVENT POSTER _________________ Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Claudine Chalmers | French Eyes on the Gold Rush – Artists and Chroniclers witness early California's astonishing transformation
events.description:
Long before the frenzy of the 1849 Gold Rush, French explorers such as the Comte de La Pérouse visited and charted the coast of California. They were followed by French diplomats in Monterey, notably Jacques-Antoine Moerenhout, whose official reports documented the early discovery of gold and the extraordinary changes it set in motion. Beginning in 1849, the Gold Rush brought a new wave of French emigrants to California, drawn by the dream of El Dorado. These fortune seekers—who came to be known as "Argonauts," after the adventurers of Greek mythology—did more than search for gold. A remarkable number of them observed, wrote, sketched, and recorded what they saw, aware that they were witnessing an extraordinary moment in history. Through travel accounts, letters, journals, and drawings, these French-speaking witnesses captured the unruly excitement of San Francisco, the hardships and disappointments of life in the mining camps, and the cultural encounters—and collisions—of a new cosmopolitan society taking shape almost overnight. Their distinctive perspective, shaped by European traditions, a critical eye, and a certain Romantic sensibility, complements the accounts of French diplomats and earlier explorers. Together, these voices offer a vivid and surprisingly rich record of what California felt and looked like as it transformed almost overnight into one of the most dynamic places in the West. Born in Cannes, Claudine Chalmers, Ph.D., is a historian, author, and independent researcher. Her passion for art, history, and the American West led her to dedicate several decades to tracing the lives of the French men and women who left for California in the 19th century. Her work include Chronicling the West for Harper's, and Splendide Californie!
Drawing on archives in France and the United States, she seeks to breathe new life into figures whom history has gradually forgotten—artists, explorers, pioneers, and adventurers whose stories reveal a French presence in the American West far richer than is commonly imagined. events.title: Dissertation Talk: Enforcing Least Privilege in the Cloud
events.description: Cloud developers increasingly hand their infrastructure and data to third-party services, such as orchestrators that launch and manage jobs, chains of services that process data on their behalf, and data lakes that store it. To do their work, these services typically receive broad access to everything a developer owns. Attackers have exploited that over-privilege in incidents ranging from the ShadowRay cluster takeovers to the Capital One breach, hijacking compute, stealing credentials, and exfiltrating data at massive scale. The principle of least privilege offers a clear fix, but today's cloud permission models cannot express it for these settings. My dissertation shows how combining proxy-based system design with cryptographic protocols makes least privilege practical without changing cloud providers or the services themselves. In this talk, I will focus on Skydentity, which enforces least privilege on third-party workload orchestrators by separating a service's ability to manage resources from its ability to access them. I will show that Skydentity reduces exposure to real-world attacks, including ShadowRay, SCARLETEEL, and cryptomining campaigns on EC2, at modest cost. I will also briefly discuss how these ideas extend to chains of services.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.
Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. A panel of land use experts and government officials from around the country will unpack the land use regimes in their states and how recent changes have—or have not—led to an increase in new housing supply. Speakers include:Christian Solorio, State Policy Campaigns Director, Welcoming Neighbors Network (Moderator) David Chiu, San Francisco City Attorney Kody Glazer, Chief Legal and Policy Officer, Florida Housing Coalition Mary Kyle McCurdy, Associate Director, 1000 Friends of Oregon The Terner Center's work on land use has been made possible through support from Arnold Ventures, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, and the National Housing Crisis Task Force.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Miryam Sas
events.description: Ela Sas is a proud young Jewish lawyer in Poland in 1939 when the war breaks out. At 4'11", she doesn't look like a force to be reckoned with. Yet when her husband and mother are killed by the Nazis, she takes off her yellow Star of David and escapes with her two-year-old baby girl, hiding her identity and pretending to be Christian. In Milk in an Eggshell (Amsterdam Publishers, 2026), compiled by Ela's granddaughter, Miryam Sas (Comparative Literature and Film & Media), Ela's stories tell us how she faced life on the other side of the unspeakable. She saw what others refused to believe and managed to survive, one act of goodwill or good luck at a time. Her story illuminates the rise of authoritarianism in terrifying detail, and shows its lingering effects. When Ela tells her granddaughter these stories, one hidden truth leads to another. The granddaughter searches for the keys to her own past — including finding her lost brother, given away at birth because he had Down syndrome. What emerges in Milk in an Eggshell is a story of empathy, connection, and healing. Sas is in conversation with Arts & Humanities dean Sara Guyer.

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Ivan Diaz (NYU Grossman School of Medicine)
events.description:
We are pleased to welcome Iván Diaz (https://med.nyu.edu/faculty/ivan-l-diaz), Associate Professor in the Division of Biostatistics at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, for CTML's Seminar on Wednesday, December 2nd. He will be presenting his talk, "Longitudinal Causal Inference Under Informative Missingness Using the Self-Censoring Model." The seminar will take place at 12:00 PM in Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401, with Iván presenting remotely.
Abstract: Longitudinal observational data are often subject to informative missingness. For example, in healthcare research using electronic health records, covariates and outcomes are measured only when patients interact with the healthcare system. Whether these data are observed usually depends on the unobserved variable values themselves, introducing a common form of data missing not at random. We develop identification and estimation methods for the effects of longitudinal modified treatment policies under a self-censoring model which explicitly models this dependence. We study two settings: one in which the observed history suffices for treatment confounding control, and another in which confounder control requires covariate values that were not measured at missed visits. In both settings, we obtain recursive identification formulas for the counterfactual outcome mean under a self-censoring model. We derive gradients of the pathwise derivatives and second-order remainder expansions, and use these results to construct estimators that accommodate machine learning for nuisance-function estimation. Under suitable product-rate conditions and cross-fitting, the estimators are asymptotically linear and permit √n inference, including simultaneous inference across outcome times. We provide numerical studies.
Bio: Iván Diaz is an Associate Professor in the Division of Biostatistics at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. His research lies at the intersection of causal inference, machine learning, and mathematical statistics, with applications in clinical, biomedical, and population health research. He develop methods to understand the causes of health and disease, the mechanisms through which they operate, and how their effects vary across individuals and populations.

events.title: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein: The Hot Mess of AI: How Does Misalignment Scale With Model Intelligence, Task Complexity, and Multiple Agents
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Wednesday, December 2, 2026 Time: 12:00pm Location: 101 Weill Hall Speaker: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein (https://sohldickstein.com/) Affiliation: Anthropic

events.title: Karl Vachuska: "Segregation and Assortative Mating: Are Changing Populations Knitting Together New Neighborhoods?"
events.description:
Abstract: America is growing more diverse: the non-White share of the population is rising, interracial marriage has become far more common, and a growing share of children are born to parents of different races. Yet American neighborhoods remain deeply segregated by race. What does the rise of interracial families mean for the future of residential segregation? This talk centers on a largely overlooked demographic process: where newly formed families settle. Using large-scale birth records linked to longitudinal residential histories, it examines the interdependent but asymmetric relationship between racial segregation and interracial family formation. Neighborhood racial composition shapes interracial family formation only weakly. Interracial family formation, by contrast, powerfully shapes the neighborhood racial composition experienced by the next generation. Interracial families loosen segregation's hold on the next generation, but they remain far less common than the same-race families through which existing residential patterns are largely reproduced.
Bio: Karl Vachuska is a PhD candidate in Sociology at UW-Madison. He studies complex systems and how they shape core processes in urban sociology, demography, and criminology. Karl integrates novel data sources with advanced methods from statistics and computer science to show how innovation in measurement and estimation can reveal central mechanisms of socioeconomic and racial inequality in health, economic mobility, segregation, and incarceration. His research has appeared in Science Advances, Demography, Social Problems, Social Networks, and Nature Scientific Reports among others.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Vivian Irish | Thorny questions: citrus development and disease
events.description: Thorns are plant defensive structures that arise from axillary shoot apical meristems that proliferate for a time and then terminally differentiate into a sharp hard tip. Like other meristems, thorn meristems contain stem cells but, in the case of thorns, these stem cells undergo a programmed cessation of proliferative activity. Using citrus as a model system to examine this unusual form of stem cell regulation, we have characterized a transcriptional gene network necessary for thorn development. Not only has this work illuminated some of the molecular mechanisms controlling plant stem cell activity, but the methods we have developed have allowed us to tackle some of the challenges facing citrus agriculture today.

events.title: Agro-pastoral Production and the Reshaping of Territoriality in Bronze-Iron Age South Caucasus
events.description:
This talk will take place in person at the ARF and on Zoom.
Register for online attendance here. (https://bit.ly/ARFtalks-2627) About: In the South Caucasus the trajectory towards sociopolitical complexity emerged in mobile communities of the Middle Bronze Age (ca. 2500-1550 BCE). At the end of this period a new form of complex, partially sedentary polities controlled from hilltop forts emerged in the region and persisted through the Late Bronze and early Iron Ages. This talk presents zooarchaeological and biogeochemical data derived from animal offerings in monumental burials (kurgans) and settlement refuse at Qızqala in Naxçıvan Autonomous Republic, Azerbaijan. These data are used to evaluate whether the community maintained spatially consistent herding practices and consider the implications for how MBA mobile pastoralism and agropastoral production shaped the subsequent Late Bronze Age regional political system.

events.title: IPSR Colloquium: Nicole Holliday, "AI as Language Police: Linguistic Surveillance and the Problem of Idealized Speech"
events.location: Room 1102 Berkeley Way West, 2121 Berkeley Way, Berkeley, CA 94704, USA
events.description: Nicole HollidayAssociate Professor of LinguisticsUniversity of California, BerkeleyAI as Language Police: Linguistic Surveillance and the Problem of Idealized Speech Linguists take it as axiomatic that speakers are experts on their languages, both in grammar and usage. However, as Large Language Models (LLM) trained on text and speech become ubiquitous in domains from daily tasks to education and employment, human expertise about language is increasingly devalued. This talk will present the results of three studies that focus on LLMs that are designed to evaluate and "improve" the speech of human talkers; these systems are known as Socially Prescriptive Speech Technologies (SPSTs). Taken together, these studies show that "AI"-based programs that purport to evaluate and transform human speech do so without consideration of linguistic principles or acknowledgement of speakers' sociolinguistic competencies. Such systems also act without transparency for both designers and users by design, reproducing social stereotypes inherent to their training data. As such technologies are already being used to make employment decisions, provide speech therapy, and even draft police reports, the fact that these systems systematically misevaluate speech represents a significant threat to all people, but most especially those from marginalized groups. Nicole Holliday is an Associate Professor of Linguistics at UC Berkeley. She received her PhD from New York University, and subsequently held positions at Pomona College and the University of Pennsylvania before joining Berkeley in 2024. Her research interests include sociophonetics, prosodic variation, speech technology, and linguistic discrimination. Her work has appeared in a variety of journals including Journal of Sociophonetics, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, Laboratory Phonology, and PLoS One. She also frequently provides media commentary on linguistics to venues such as the New York Times, The Guardian, and the San Francisco Chronicle, and she posts about language on Tiktok: @mixedlinguist.
