events.title: Restless Ground: Lilah Nethanel on Writing Israel
events.description:
Helen Diller Institute Literary Series, Session II*Co-sponsored by the Center for Jewish Studies and the Department of Comparative Literature, UC Berkeley What can a sleepless man reveal about the history of a country, and what forgotten paths might Hebrew literature have taken? Israeli novelist and literary scholar Lilah Nethanel approaches some of Hebrew literature's most familiar and contested subjects—home, land, desire, language, and belonging—from startlingly unexpected angles. In The Tired Ones, one man's longing for sleep opens onto Israel's fraught histories of land and ownership, while Works and Days compresses fifteen years of marriage, desire, and betrayal into two hours of an ordinary summer evening. Her newly published study, The Last European-Hebrew Writer, returns to David Frishman to recover two possibilities for modern Hebrew culture that once coexisted: a European-Hebrew literature centered in Warsaw and a Hebrew-Arabic literature emerging in Ottoman Jerusalem. In conversation with Yael Segalovitz, Nethanel will explore how intimate lives and forgotten literary alternatives can unsettle the familiar stories Israel tells about itself.
Lilah Nethanel, Literary scholar and Israeli novelist; Senior Lecturer, Department of Literature, Bar-Ilan UniversityYael Segalovitz, Joan Bieder Visiting Professor of Jewish and Hebrew Literature, Helen Diller Institute, UC Berkeley; Comparative Literature Department, UC Berkeley; Assistant Professor, Ben-Gurion University of the NegevRegister: https://HDILitSeries2.rsvpify.com (https://hdilitseries2.rsvpify.com)

events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: Total Collision and Eigenvalues
events.description: Speaker: Richard Montgomery, UC Santa CruzAbstract: Any solution to the classical N-body problem ending in total collision does so with some limiting shape. This limiting shape is known as a `central configuration' and the number of distinct central configurations is believed to be finite for all N and known to be finite for N = 3 an 4. For the spatial 4-body problem we prove that if that limiting shape is planar then the entire solution lies in a fixed plane in space. The method of proof begins with McGehee blow-up which extends the N-body flow to a "collision manifold" whose equilibrium points are in 2:1 correspondence with the central configurations, where one of these `2' represents solutions coming in to total collision and the other represents solutions exploding out of total collision. The analysis and proof then boils down to linearizing the flow at a planar equilibrium, understanding the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the resulting linear operator, and combining this information with a kind of watered-down geometric version of the center manifold theorem. A curious feature is that the eigenvalues of the linearization are not those of a Hamiltonian vector field at equilibrium, despite the fact that the vector field encoding Newton's 4-body problem is (conformally) symplectic away from the collision manifold. This is joint work with Guowei Yu of the Chern Institute in Tianjin and a preliminary version is available at arXiv:2609.32088.

events.title: Care in Our Backyard: Domesticating the Market and Commercializing the Home in 1980s California
events.description: For much of the 20th century, the mixing of domestic and market life by turning homes into sites of production, commerce, or speculation was seen as a threat to family life and its economic security. These practices were stigmatized as racialized informality, regulated by armies of labor, land-use, and code enforcement inspectors, and pathologized for promoting an aberrant domesticity and child labor. However, since the 1970s, diverse forms of what I term "home-based moneymaking" have not only proliferated, but perceptions of them have shifted too. This talk will consider two cases: so-called "granny flats" (accessory dwelling units in single-family homes) and "family day care" (home-based child care). These forms of contested home-based informality were incorporated in the 1980s as state legislatures sought a third way, between public and market provision, to address crises of affordable housing and care. But both also constituted the earliest modern cases in which state regulators overrode municipalities' zoning restrictions on non-residential uses. I will trace how state legislators promoted these enabling laws by portraying the practices as extensions of the domestic sphere, rather than the commercialization of homes. Luis Flores is a historical sociologist engaged in economic, urban/regional, and social inequality research. His research examines the regulatory and social politics surrounding home-based moneymaking, as previously stigmatized forms of informality became increasingly popular.

events.title: 2026 Berkeley Bioengineering Distinguished Lecture with Clifford Brangwynne, PhD
events.description: Fluid Machinery: The Nucleolus, Ribosomes, and Aging Abstract: Research combining insights from materials physics and cell biology has ushered in a new paradigm for understanding how the chaotic intracellular environment is brought to order, through the collective condensation of biomolecules into droplets of living information. In this talk, I will present an overview of these principles and ongoing work in this field, with a particular emphasis on the interplay between liquid-like condensates and traditional biomolecular machines, such as the ribosome, which forms through a complex assembly process in the multiphase nucleolus. Our lab has recently developed a set of tools to probe and engineer the nucleolus and the production of ribosomes, as well as their cytoplasmic function in protein translation. These studies are yielding new insights into how assembled ribosomes function in space and time, and how ribosomes can become dysregulated by molecular and organismal aging.

events.title: EECS Colloquium | Pursuing a "Moore's Law" for Power Electronics
events.description: As processors and controllers of electrical energy, power electronics are key drivers of innovation in transportation, energy systems, aerospace, computing, manufacturing, healthcare, consumer electronics, and more. However, unlike information-processing circuits, power electronics are challenging to miniaturize and have yet to undergo the extreme scaling that underpins microelectronics today. While major advances have been enabled by advanced semiconductor devices and control capabilities, further progress is now primarily bottlenecked by the energy storage components they depend on, particularly magnetics (i.e., inductors and transformers). Dramatic miniaturization of power electronics will therefore require new approaches to power conversion with superior power density and performance at small sizes. This talk explores how we can leverage an alternative energy storage modality – electromechanical energy storage in piezoelectric resonators – to unlock a new era of scalability for power electronics. Unlike magnetics, piezoelectric resonators offer power densities that fundamentally improve as they shrink, among numerous other advantages in size, performance, and manufacturability. Realizing these advantages, however, will require new design strategies for both power electronic circuits and the resonators themselves. Accordingly, this talk will present recent advances in (1) circuit topologies and control for resonator-based dc-dc converters and "active inductors", and (2) piezoelectric component design concepts including isolated piezoelectric transformers and "overtone" piezoelectric resonators. These strategies enable high-performance use of piezoelectric resonators as energy storage components across a wide range of applications, laying a foundation for power electronics that scale favorably to small sizes. Jessica Boles is the Chenming Hu Assistant Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences at the University of California, Berkeley, and inaugural Co-Director of the Berkeley Power and Energy Center. She received her B.S. and M.S. degrees from the University of Tennessee, Knoxville (UTK) and her Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), all in electrical engineering. Boles' research pursues major advances in the performance, size, and cost of power electronics through use of alternative passive component technologies. Her research interests span power converter circuit topologies, modeling, and control, as well as passive component design, modeling, fabrication, and characterization. Boles has received the ARPA-E IGNIITE Award, the NASA Early Career Faculty Award, the NSF CAREER Award, and the UCOP Early Career Faculty Research Excellence Award. Her work has been recognized with three IEEE prize paper awards and the IEEE PELS Ph.D. Thesis Talk Award. She currently serves on the leadership of two technical committees in the IEEE Power Electronics Society: Emerging Technologies and Control and Modeling of Power Electronics.

events.title: ERG Colloquium Series Fall 2026: Steven Ostoja
events.description:
Title: Science in Service of Decisions: Reducing Wildfire Risk, Building ResilienceTalk Abstract: How can decision-relevant science help safeguard California's ecosystems and communities from devastating wildfires? Drawing on leadership from the California's Wildfire Science Synthesis and the 5th National Climate Assessment's Focus on Western Wildfires, I will examine solutions spanning forest management, beneficial fire, community planning, and postfire recovery. The talk will explore how scientific evidence can inform investments in fuel treatments, home hardening, reforestation, and protection of ecosystem services. I will also discuss the process and role of collaborative science in translating complex findings and uncertainty into practical guidance for decision makers working to reduce wildfire risk and build resilience across California's landscapes.
Bio: Steven Ostoja directs USDA's California Climate Hub and is a research scientist at Agricultural Research Service where he leads a team that connects science to service in support of agricultural productivity and forest resilience. He co-chairs the Wildfire and Landscape Resilience Task Forces Science Advisory Panel, contributes to national and state climate assessments, and helps shape reforestation strategies, including leading California's first. Steve holds a Ph.D. in Ecology from Utah State University and M.S. and B.S. degrees in Biological Sciences from Cal Poly, San Luis Obispo. An avid mountain biker and kayaker, he enjoys exploring the trails and rivers of the Sierra Nevada foothills.

events.title: MBN Seminar: Aldosterone-Independent Regulation of Potassium Handling by the Distal Nephron: a resolution to the aldosterone paradox.
events.description:
Title: Aldosterone-Independent Regulation of Potassium Handling by the Distal Nephron: a resolution to the aldosterone paradox.
Summary: Aldosterone has long been seen as the central regulator of both extracellular fluid volume and plasma K+concentration in mammals, which suggested a paradox: how does aldosterone "know" which homeostatic process to regulate. We showed more than a decade ago that the serine-threonine kinase, SGK1, which regulates both Na+ and K+ transport in kidney tubule cells, is under dual regulation: its expression level is controlled by mineralocorticoid receptor-dependent gene transcription and its catalytic activity by mTORC2-dependent phosphorylation. However, the mechanistic basis and physiologic role of this dual regulation remained obscure. We now have evidence for an mTORC2-dependent, aldosterone-independent, signaling mechanism that selectively stimulates SGK1 in K+ secretory cells, while aldosterone regulates SGK1 in Na+/Cl- reabsorbing cells. Our findings provide a basis for independent regulation of body fluid volume and K+ concentration and suggest a resolution for the aldosterone paradox.

About the Play: What happens when we decide we know another person better than they know themselves? Inspired by a true story, Boy follows the life and relationships of Adam, whose family chose to raise him as a girl following an early medical accident–as advised by his doctor. Boy is a play built around the freedom to create one's identity, the dynamics of control within relationships, and the consequences of choices one was never allowed to make. As performance laboratories, workshops provide opportunities for student directors, choreographers, writers, and performers to develop ideas and put them into practice. Performances focus on engaging language and staging with minimal technical/design elements.

events.title: Dave Pagliarini: Mining mitochondria—proteins, pathways, and pathogenesis
events.description:
Despite their iconic status in cell biology, mitochondria remain surprisingly mysterious. These organelles harbor hundreds of uncharacterized "orphan" proteins and are linked to a vast array of physiological processes, often through unclear means. Many well-known mitochondrial activities rely on enzymes, chaperones, and transporters yet to be identified. Mitochondrial dysfunction underlies hundreds of rare diseases, yet nearly half lack molecular diagnoses and there remains but two FDA-approved drugs to treat them. My talk will cover how we aim to clarify this remarkable opacity by blending new systematic methods with rigorous mechanistic biochemistry and chemical biology to discover new protein activities, link them to new biology and unresolved diseases, and manipulate them through customized small molecule interventions.
Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Johannes Blom (Karolinska Institutet)
events.description:
Come and be part of our last seminar discussion for the Fall Semester on December 3rd! Johannes Blom, Colorectal Surgeon at Södersjukhuset and Researcher at Karolinska Institutet, will present his talk on "Can Real-World Data Help Us Develop Better Colorectal Cancer Screening Strategies and Policies?" The talk will take place at 12:00 PM at Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401.
Abstract: Colorectal cancer screening reduces cancer incidence and mortality, yet many fundamental questions remain unanswered. Should screening start and stop at the same age for everyone? Should screening intervals and decisions following a positive stool-based screening test for blood be adapted according to an individual's screening history and health profile? And can we reduce unnecessary colonoscopies while maintaining the benefits of screening? Drawing on one of the world's largest real-world colorectal cancer screening cohorts, including more than 400,000 individuals linked to longitudinal healthcare, prescription, socioeconomic, and cancer registry data in Sweden, this seminar explores how large-scale observational data can help address clinically important questions that are difficult or impossible to answer through randomized trials alone. Using examples from ongoing research, the talk will discuss opportunities and challenges in developing more effective and resource-efficient approaches to colorectal cancer prevention. Bio: Johannes Blom, MD, PhD, is a colorectal surgeon at Södersjukhuset and researcher at Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, Sweden. His research focuses on colorectal cancer prevention, screening, endoscopy quality, and the use of nationwide healthcare data to improve clinical decision-making and population health. Dr. Blom leads research based on Sweden's population-based colorectal cancer screening programs and collaborates with colleagues in Scandinavia and the United States to develop innovative approaches to precision cancer prevention using real-world data.

events.title: From dispersal to divergence: exploring the many faces of allopatric speciation
events.description: Freshwater fishes of eastern North America, particularly darters, are an exceptional system for studying the mechanisms and outcomes of allopatric speciation, given their high regional diversity and strong habitat specificity. Allopatric speciation is predicted to leave sister species in separate but adjacent river systems; yet a time-calibrated phylogeny of nearly all 290 darter species, combined with genomic species delimitation, reveals far more varied outcomes. Some sister lineages achieve secondary sympatry rapidly, while others persist in deep allopatry, never overlapping even with distant relatives, raising questions about why lineages differ in their transition rates from isolation to co-occurrence. At finer scales, case studies of recently delimited species complexes identify multiple drivers of allopatric speciation, including dispersal into newly available habitat and ecological divergence along resource axes like diet and substrate, extending well beyond classic vicariance models. This work establishes a research program linking speciation mechanisms to their long-term geographic and ecological consequences, contrasted with dynamics of island and lake adaptive radiations.

events.title: CCB Seminar: Pilar Cossio, Senior Research Scientist, Flatiron Institute
events.description:
Title: Inferring Biomolecular Ensembles from Cryo-EM Images with Physical and Generative PriorsAbstract: Biomolecules are dynamic, and understanding their function requires characterizing not just individual structures but entire conformational ensembles and their populations. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) captures noisy snapshots of individual molecules, providing direct experimental access to these ensembles, yet extracting them remains challenging. In this talk, I will present a unified framework for ensemble inference in which prior knowledge, either from molecular dynamics (MD) force fields or pretrained diffusion models, is integrated by cryo-EM data. With MD, we bias simulations using a likelihood computed directly from particle images, jointly inferring structures and population weights without a pre-sampled ensemble. With diffusion models, we guide generation toward experimental data, including by optimizing the model's conditioning to shift the prior itself. Applied to proteins and RNAs, these approaches recover multiple conformational states and their populations from synthetic and experimental data, opening the way to ensemble-level quantitative structural biology of flexible biomolecules.
Bio:Pilar Cossio has worked at the Flatiron Institute, Center for Computational Mathematics, since 2021 as the Research Scientist and Project Leader for Biomolecular and Biophysical Inference (BBI). Previously, Cossio was Max Planck Tandem Group Leader associated with the University of Antioquia (Colombia) and the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics (Germany). She also has held postdoctoral positions at the National Institute of Health (NIH, USA) and the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics. Cossio focuses on the development of mathematical and computational methods to characterize proteins' structures and dynamics from cryo-electron microscopy, single-molecule spectroscopy and biomolecular simulations. Cossio holds a Ph.D. in Physics and Chemistry of Biological Systems from the International School for Advanced Studies (SISSA) in Italy and a B.S. in Physics from the University of Antioquia.

events.title: Alexander Nectow: Neuronal control of the heart
events.description: Stress is a major trigger of arrhythmias, yet the mechanisms underlying these effects remain poorly defined. While adrenergic signaling is critical for rhythm disturbances in vulnerable hearts, the central neuronal mechanisms responsible for this maladaptive drive are largely unknown. Using a genetic model of ventricular tachycardia (VT), we find that naturalistic emotional stressors rapidly provoke malignant arrhythmias in vulnerable hearts. By tracing back from sympathetic neurons innervating myocardium, we identify a multi-synaptic, brain-to-heart circuit originating within the midbrain periaqueductal gray, which is required for stress-induced VT. Strikingly, activation of this pathway induces VT within seconds, suggesting that central neuronal control of the heart is an important arrhythmogenic trigger. Together, this work identifies a brain-to-heart circuit responsible for triggering stress-induced arrhythmias and points toward neural circuit-directed therapies for cardiovascular disease.

events.title: Astronomy Colloquium - Alyssa Goodman (Harvard)
events.description:
Title: Mysterious Motions of Molecular Gas in M83Abstract: M83 (NGC 5236), only about 4.9 Mpc away from Earth, and seen tipped nearly face-on, offers one of the best available views of how gas moves in a grand-design spiral galaxy. Using ALMA CO(1–0) observations of the full molecular disk, we subtract an empirical "blanket" model of smooth, large-scale velocity structure (including rotation) and examine what remains. The residual velocity field contains a wealth of structure on scales from a few hundred parsecs to kiloparsecs, organized by the spiral pattern, whose relationship to in-plane streaming and to vertical motion we test directly. We search for and analyze analogous structure in a companion simulation. We discuss what these organized motions, many not previously mapped in detail over a full galactic disk, imply about the three-dimensional dynamics of spirals — including how they could relate to the Radcliffe Wave, other vertical oscillations seen in the Milky Way, and tugs from a huge reservoir of atomic gas beyond the CO disk — and what a face-on external galaxy can tell us that our own cannot. The talk will include a discussion of the very positive and very negative roles of AI in this research to-date.
Host: Jessica Lu

events.title: Creativity and Playwriting: A Conversation with Stan Lai
events.description:
What does it take to create a theatrical masterpiece? Where do great ideas come from, and how do playwrights transform them into unforgettable experiences onstage? Join us for a special conversation with internationally acclaimed playwright, director, and UC Berkeley alumnus Stan Lai (Ph.D. Dramatic Art '83), one of the most influential voices in contemporary theater. Hosted by TDPS Department Chair Abigail De Kosnik and TDPS Professor Lisa Wymore, this conversation will explore Lai's creative process, the evolution of his groundbreaking body of work, and his journey from graduate student at UC Berkeley to internationally celebrated theatermaker. Lai's Secret Love in Peach Blossom Land was recently named by The New York Times as one of the essential works of theater of the past 100 years. Drawing on decades of artistic innovation, Lai will share insights into the art and craft of playwriting, reflect on his past and current projects, and offer inspiration and advice to the next generation of theatermakers, artists, and storytellers.
About Stan Lai: Stan Lai (Lai Shengchuan) has been called "The best Chinese language playwright and director in the world" (BBC) and "Asia's top theatre director." (Asiaweek) Robert Brustein considered him "unchallenged as the major contemporary Asian playwright of his time, perhaps of all time." Lai was born in Washington, DC in 1954, and grew up in the US and Taiwan. After receiving his PhD in Dramatic Art at Berkeley in 1983, Lai began his creative journey in Taipei, Taiwan, creating bold new plays that brought audiences into the theatre, at a time when there was no organized theatre industry. Over the decades, many a Chinese-speaking theatregoer's first experience of theatre has been a play of Stan Lai's. To date he has written and directed over 40 original full length plays, including those regarded as masterpieces of the modern Chinese-language theatre such as Secret Love in Peach Blossom Land (1986, chosen by the New York Times in 2026 as one of the "Essential Plays of the Past 100 Years"), The Village (2008, called "The pinnacle of theatre in our time" by the Beijing News), and A Dream Like A Dream (2000, called by China Daily "possibly the greatest Chinese-language play since time immemorial.") Lai's awards include Taiwan's National Arts Award an unprecedented twice. He was also awarded a star on the Walk of Fame at the Sibiu International Theatre Festival. Lai is also an award-winning feature filmmaker and acclaimed opera and events director, as well as a noted theatre educator, having taught over two decades at Taipei National university of the Arts, and also at Stanford, Berkeley, CalArts and the Shanghai Theatre Academy. Two of Lai's most acclaimed works, A Dream Like A Dream and AGO were created in workshop form while teaching at Berkeley. Lai's publications in English include Selected Plays of Stan Lai (3 vols, 12 plays in his own English translations, U. of Michigan Press, 2022) and Creativitry: Asia's Iconic Playwright Reveals the Art of Creativity (Anthem, 2025), the English version of his groundbreaking Chinese work on creativity, which has sold over one million copies. Lai is currently Artistic Director of Performance Workshop, Taiwan, and Theatre Above, Shanghai, a venue dedicated to the performance of his works, as well as Artistic Founder of the Huichang Theatre Village. He is Co-founder, Festival Director and Jury Head of the Wuzhen Theatre Festival.

events.title: Fall 2026 Senior Thesis Exhibition Opening Reception
events.location: Worth Ryder Art Gallery, Anthropology and Art Building, Rm 116. Near the intersection of College Ave. & Bancroft Way
events.description: Worth Ryder Art Gallery and the Department of Art Practice are excited to announce Windows to Here, the Department of Art Practice's Fall 2026 Senior Thesis Exhibition featuring multidisciplinary artworks by seventeen Art Practice majors. Fog covers and clears over a distant view of the Golden Gate Bridge. A jogger runs by, pulled by his dog. A family sits down to dinner. A cat curls up on a sill. A dog peers out expectantly. A professor lectures to a room full of students. A friend walks by on their way to class. Rain pours down and I reach to close my window. Are artworks windows into artists' understandings of the world? The Fall 2026 Senior Thesis Exhibition Windows to Here frames seventeen different artists' views of spaces, experiences, aspirations and imaginaries through the mediums of painting, sculpture, printmaking and installation. These student artists gaze inward toward personal identity, childhood, and inherited histories, and they look outward toward cultural belonging, migration, labor, and the environments we live in. Rather than offering a single perspective, Windows to Here invites viewers to encounter the many ways we see and experience the world we share. What do you see through the window? Windows to Here features artworks by students in Brody Reiman and Anne Walsh's ART185 Senior Projects/Professional Practices classes, supported by Graduate Student Instructor Lorain Khalil Rihan. Artists: Mika Rose Alven, Deniz Gül Avci, Nora Buchanan, Sam Chen, Ian Frigon, Lindsey Hiner, Violet Jones, Kari Lee, Yiyang (Helen) Liu, Rene Barba Lopez, SAINT LUI, Flor Aleli Santiago, Amira Thomas, Grace Vierra, Jose Yahir Villicaña Ordaz, Collette Wilson, Ian Yuan Opening reception: Thursday, December 3, 4pm - 6pmExhibition dates: Tuesday, December 1 - Friday, December 11Gallery Hours during this exhibition: Monday/Wednesday: 1pm-6pm Tuesday/Thursday: 12pm-6pm Friday: 1pm-5pm Saturday/Sunday: Closed Worth Ryder Art Gallery, UC Berkeley Anthropology and Art Practice Building, Rm 116 Near the intersection of College Ave and Bancroft Way Poster design by Zia Daniels

events.title: Lecture | The Art of Not Governing: Muslims as Unincorporated Populations in Early Modern East-Central Europe
events.description:
The Center for Middle Eastern Studies, The Institute of European Studies, and the Institute of Slavic, East European, and Eurasian Studies present a lecture with Dr. David Do Paço of the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs.
Abstract: In early modern Christian-ruled Europe, unincorporated populations, Muslims in particular, compensated for their lack of administrative protection by cultivating diverse circles of social belonging: circles that overlapped imperfectly, complemented one another, and sometimes conflicted. Foucault and Scott have emphasized the administrative violence of early modern states, rooted in their inability to read society and their tendency to reduce it to rigid communities. This talk instead explores why eighteenth-century administrations had an interest in letting unincorporated populations prosper, and how Muslims became agents of the economic expansion and radical transformation of the early modern world, with a specific focus on the Habsburg Lands and Danubian territories. Rather than viewing non-incorporation as exclusion, the talk argues that administrative indifference could be a deliberate strategy, allowing states to benefit from mobile commercial networks, frontier expertise, and cross-border ties they could neither control nor replace. Unincorporated status thus emerges as a productive space where social belonging was continually redefined.
Speaker Bio: David Do Paço is an early modern historian and a diplomat. He earned his PhD in 2012 from Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne with a dissertation on the Ottoman commercial-cum-political milieu of eighteenth-century Vienna. The resulting book, L’Orient à Vienne au dix-huitième siècle, was published by the Voltaire Foundation in 2015. He has since held positions at the European University Institute, Sciences Po, where he ran the Departmental seminar in European History, and Columbia University, where he chaired East Central European Studies in 2021, as the Istvan Deák Visiting Professor. His research, at the intersection of social, urban, and political history, has appeared in international journals, including Urban History, the Historical Journal or Business History. In 2023, he joined the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs as the inaugural Attaché for Academic Cooperation in San Francisco, where he works to strengthen ties between French and American universities.

events.title: "Heavy Abstraction" by Luke Fidler
events.description:
"Heavy Abstraction" by Luke FidlerAbstract: How did sculpture shape the practices of premodern metrology? And how, in turn, did the material and conceptual conditions of non-monetary exchange shape the making of sculpture? This talk explores these questions by examining weights made during the long ninth century to evaluate precious metal objects in the bullion economy of northern Europe. Formed by dismembering and reassembling works of sculpture, these weights constitute the primary archive of a lost corpus of early-medieval figural art from the British Isles. But reading against the art historical grain shows them to be remarkably self-reflexive miniature sculptures in their own right, produced through acts of economic and collective violence then cast into the maritime networks of northern Europe. There, I argue that their fragmentary aesthetic thematized judgment's most relational features; art, rather than some sovereign authority, offered a standard of value to the world.
Bio: Luke Fidler is assistant professor of art history at the University of Southern California, where his research focuses on the art and political economy of the European Middle Ages. His work has been supported by the Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts at the National Gallery of Art, the Society for the Humanities at Cornell University, and the Henry Moore Foundation, and his articles have recently appeared in The Art Bulletin, Critical Inquiry, Gesta,Representations, Res, and Texte zur Kunst. Committed to the emancipatory resources of art history, he has taught with community and prison teaching initiatives including the Prison+Neighborhood Arts/Education Project and the Odyssey Project; he also worked as curator and program manager of the Mellon-funded 'Visualizing Abolition' project at UC Santa Cruz. During 2026-27, he is writing a book about the art of orientation in the early-medieval north Atlantic while a member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. events.title: Amara Ali | Beyond Delhi and Lucknow: The Lives of Urdu in Twentieth-Century Kashmir
events.description:
A talk by Amara Ali, (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) Lecturer in Urdu, Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, that examines twentieth-century Kashmir as a distinctive center of Urdu literary culture through the evolution of Shia marṣiya.
Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, December 3, 2026 (NEW DATE) TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: On FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) —————- ABSTRACT The history of Urdu has largely been told through its major centers, Delhi and Lucknow, with other regions positioned as peripheral recipients of a tradition formed elsewhere. This talk turns to Kashmir to complicate that geography, taking the twentieth century as its focus. This was a period in which Kashmir developed its own robust institutions of Urdu literary production and appreciation, from madrasas and administrative offices to mushāʿira gatherings and radio broadcasts. Multilingualism has long been part and parcel of Kashmiri intellectual and cultural life, with different languages holding prominence in different periods: Sanskrit, then Persian, and eventually Urdu. To trace how this played out in the twentieth century, the talk turns to Kashmiri Shia marṣiya, a devotional genre, and its jadīd (modern) forms, which register this movement between languages and make visible Kashmir's own productive engagement with Urdu. SPEAKER BIOAmara Ali (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) is a Lecturer in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies. Her research centers on the interplay of Urdu, Hindi, and Kashmiri literary traditions and Islam in South Asia. Her doctoral dissertation provides a literary examination of the Kashmiri marsiya (an elegiac poem), analyzing how this local form articulates a unique Kashmiri aesthetic, while remaining in critical dialogue with the broader Urdu, Persian, and Arabic literary traditions. Earlier, she completed her master's studies at the University of Cambridge, focusing on the celebrated Urdu poets Mirza Ghalib and Faiz Ahmed Faiz.

events.title: Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Myungji Yang (University of Hawai'i, Mānoa) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance: https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_5Ug1zjOPToSo9aTktNXqNg (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_5Ug1zjOPToSo9aTktNXqNg) Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The rise of the illiberal, far-right politics threatens democratic system throughout the world. The South Korean president Yoon Seok-yeol's martial law declaration in December 2024 stunned the world. More puzzling is that Yoon's insurrection unexpectedly gained substantial support from the ruling right-wing party and ordinary citizens. Why do ordinary citizens support authoritarian leaders and martial law in a democratic country? What draws these citizens to extreme actions and ideas? Through eighteen months of field research and drawing from rich qualitative data, this talk will provide an in-depth account of the ideas and practices of the far-right groups and organizations, and help to understand the roots of current democratic regression. Speaker Bio: Myungji Yang is Professor of Sociology at the University of Hawai'i-Mānoa. A political sociologist and social movement scholar, she is interested in the issues of power, inequality, civil society and democracy. Her research has appeared in Nations and Nationalism, Politics and Society, Mobilization: An International Inquiry, Urban Studies, and Sociological Inquiry, among other venues. Arlie Hochschild has spent a decade thinking and writing about communities on the political right. For her bestselling Strangers in Their Own Land (2016), she embedded in Lousiana's Calcasieu Parish to help explain the Tea Party to Americans who were bewildered by it. Eight years later, she returned with Stolen Pride, about Pikeville, Kentucky—a MAGA stronghold in one of the country's whitest and poorest congressional districts. A New York Times Best Book of the Year, it makes the case that the region's politics are driven less by policies or economics than by shame and a narrative of "stolen" pride. Join California magazine's Pat Joseph in conversation with Hochschild as they discuss what she's learned from her time amongst Donald Trump's supporters and how that knowledge might help us mend our fractured democracy. Established in 1991 by June Jordan and rooted in her work in the departments of African American Studies and Gender and Women's Studies at UC Berkeley, Poetry for the People (P4P) taught students to speak their truth through poetry. Today, with the clarity and political commitment of June's vision more necessary than ever, "Poetry for the People: A Blueprint for the Future" asks, how do we teach P4P now? "Poetry for the People: A Blueprint for the Future" is a convening intended for UC Berkeley faculty, students, and staff; P4P program alumni; P4P instructors; community partners; and anyone committed to the future of P4P at UC Berkeley and beyond. The day-long program will include workshops about the history and legacy of P4P, how P4P is being taught today, and new models of P4P for the modern university. events.title: Dissertation Talk: From Perception to Action to Interaction: Deep Data for Robot Learning
events.description: Internet-scale data has made large vision and language models remarkably general, while the lack of a comparable corpus in robotics has long bottlenecked similar progress. In this talk, I argue that beyond just sheer scale of data that can be downloaded and passively consumed, robots need "deep data," which exists only once they act: where their behavior leads and what their actions physically induce. I will present my work on various pieces of this puzzle, building towards a recipe for scalable robot learning in the real world. I will begin with perception, drawing on passively observed and generatively synthesized data to ask how far learning without acting can go. I will then move to action, where curiosity and generative models of experience help agents learn from the consequences of their own behavior, first in simulation and then in the real world. Finally, I will address interaction during deployment, where foundation models and reusable skills let a robot turn its own failures into corrective experience, improving without new demonstrations. Together, these works sketch a recipe for scalable robot learning: broad data and generative models to build priors and stretch experience, and real-world action to gather the deep data which only interaction can provide.

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Prof. Valla Fatemi, Cornell University | Toward Robust Superconducting Quantum Computation: From Nanofabrication to Logical Control
events.description: Abstract: Superconducting circuits are a leading hardware platform for quantum computation. The way to fabricate the devices, arrange them, and then control them in operando remains a major open question. In any implementation, we desire physical devices that preserve coherence as long as possible alongside robust logical operations. In this talk, I will present two complementary advances toward these goals. First, I will describe a new tantalum thin-film synthesis procedure, alongside the rest of our fabrication method, that enables high-performance superconducting qubit circuits. Our qubits are at the leading edge, with quality factors exceeding 16 million. I will then turn to protecting quantum information during computation in the context of bosonic codes. Bosonic codes encode a logical qubit in the states of a harmonic oscillator, which can offer advantages in hardware-efficiency. However, preserving protection against physical errors during logical gate operations remains a major challenge. I will introduce a framework that enables standard microwave controls to implement a universal set of single-logical-qubit gates that are approximately 'transparent' to photon loss, allowing for correction of errors after gate operations. Experiments demonstrate a five-fold reduction in gate infidelity conditioned on photon loss, and improved preservation of information during active control with error correction. Together, these efforts represent a dual-pronged effort to advance the frontier of protecting quantum information. Bio: Dr. Valla Fatemi received his PhD in Physics in the group of Pablo Jarillo-Herrero at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2018. There he worked on electronic and quantum transport in topological insulator materials, including discovery of superconductor and topological insulator states in monolayer tungsten ditelluride. He then joined the group of Michel Devoret at Yale University as the post-doctoral associate on the teams researching the physics of Andreev bound states in superconductor-semiconductor quantum devices, helping to demonstrate the first Andreev spin qubit. In 2022 he joined the faculty of the School of Applied and Engineering Physics at Cornell University, where he is building a lab researching the basic and applied physics of quantum materials, quantum control, superconducting quantum circuits, and their intersections, including a focus on materials and nanofabrication for improving superconducting qubits.

events.title: BLC Talk | Creating the Conditions for Languages to Thrive: Advocacy, Leadership, and Institutional Change | Deb Reisinger
events.description: Creating the Conditions for Languages to Thrive: Advocacy, Leadership, and Institutional Change Deb Reisinger Dean of Undergraduate Education; Trinity College, Duke University In "Creating the Conditions", Reisinger examines how content-based language programs can expand the role and reach of language study within a contemporary liberal arts education. Drawing on established approaches in Cultures and Languages Across the Curriculum (CLAC), community-based language learning (CBLL), and Languages for Specific Purposes (LSP), she considers how language courses and programs can connect linguistic development with disciplinary knowledge, critical inquiry, experiential learning, and transferable skills. Examples from undergraduate curricula illustrate the distinct possibilities of these models. CLAC integrates languages and intercultural perspectives across disciplines; CBLL creates reciprocal relationships between classroom learning and community engagement, and LSP connects language learning to professional fields and practices. Together, these approaches make visible the intellectual and practical value of language study across academic, professional, and civic contexts. This presentation also considers what allows such programs to take root and thrive. Curricular innovation depends on more than compelling individual courses. It requires faculty leadership, meaningful institutional partnerships, coherent pathways for students, and structures that support collaboration across departments, programs, and schools. It also requires clear narratives that help students, faculty colleagues, and university leaders understand how language learning advances broader institutional commitments. By bringing curricular models into conversation with questions of advocacy, leadership, and institutional design, Reisinger invites participants to consider the conditions that support language study at their own institution. Ultimately, she asks how content-based programs can help build connections, create new points of entry, and position linguistic and intercultural learning as essential dimensions of a liberal arts education. Bio: Deb Reisinger is Dean of Undergraduate Education at Duke University. A professor of French Studies and affiliate faculty in Global Health and Markets & Management, Deb directs Duke's Language Outreach Initiatives(link is external), including Cultures and Languages Across the Curriculum and the Shared Online Consortium for LCTLs. Deb's work explores the connections between language learning and the disciplines. She is lead author of Affaires globales: S'engager dans le monde professionnel en francais, niveau avancé and co-author of Community-based Language Learning, a methodology of critical service-learning in world languages. In 2022, she was named Chevalier dans l'Ordre des Palmes Académiques by the French Republic.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Towards Secure Systems with Asymmetric Distributed Trust
events.description: The security and efficiency of computer systems depend critically on their underlying trust assumptions. Distributed trust strengthens security by splitting trust across independent trust domains, while asymmetric trust improves efficiency by exploiting differences in trust assumptions. Together, these principles enable secure systems that achieve stronger security guarantees and greater efficiency. In this talk, I will present two privacy-preserving systems that leverage asymmetric distributed trust to improve security and efficiency, respectively. First, I will present Chorus, a secret recovery system that enables distributed trust across millions of unreliable, resource-constrained client devices by relying on clients for privacy but not availability. Next, I will discuss Myco, a metadata-private messaging system that unlocks sublinear per-access overhead with strong privacy guarantees by trusting one server with read access patterns and another with write access patterns.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
Stefan Minasian, Staff Chemist, LBNLThe Counterintuitive Relationship between Orbital Energy, Orbital Overlap,and Covalency in f-Element Molecules Why are some metal–ligand bonds more covalent than others? Typically, chemists invoke two factors: how well the metal and ligand orbitals overlap in space, and how closely their energies match. Yet these contributions have been surprisingly difficult to separate, by either experiment or theory. This lecture will describe how ligand K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), combined with high-level spectral simulations, can measure both. Comparisons of isostructural fluoride and chloride complexes of transition metals (Ti, Zr, Hf), lanthanides (Ce), and actinides (U, Np, Pu) show that the two factors often work against each other. Greater orbital overlap does not necessarily produce a more covalent bond, and the balance between overlap and energy matching depends on the metal and on the symmetry of the interaction. These results also provide experimental benchmarks against which computational descriptions of bonding can be tested. The second part of the lecture will extend this approach to organometallic lanthanide complexes, probed using carbon K-edge XAS. In molecules such as cerocene, Ce(C8H8)2, and Cp′3Eu, the ground state cannot be described by a single electronic configuration. In these systems, the 4f orbital mixing observed by X-ray spectroscopy also appears as partial charge transfer from the ligands to the metal. Relating these two descriptions shows how 4f electrons can participate in bonding while remaining largely localized, and how 4f covalency can shape physical properties such as magnetic susceptibility. This leads to broader questions about how covalency and multiconfigurational ground states are connected across the f-block.
The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Concert: Aiyun Huang
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description:
Performance featuring Aiyun HuangBIO: Aiyun Huang enjoys a musical life as a soloist, chamber musician, researcher, teacher and producer. Globally recognized since winning the 2002 First Prize and Audience Prize of the Geneva International Music Competition. She is a champion of existing repertoire and a prominent voice in the collaborative creation of new works. Huang has premiered over two hundred works in her three decades as a performer and producer. The Globe and Mail critic Robert Everett-Green describes Huang's playing as "engrossing to hear and to watch" and her choice of repertoire as capable of "renovating our habits of listening." Her past highlights include performances with the St. Lawrence String Quartet, L'Orchestre de la Suisse Romande, Taipei Symphony Orchestra and San Diego Symphony Orchestra. She has appeared in international festivals and venues including the Victoria Hall in Geneva, Los Angeles Philharmonic Orchestra's Green Umbrella Series, LACMA Concert Series, Holland Festival, Agora Festival in Paris, Banff Arts Festival, 7éme Biennale d'Art Contemporaine de Lyon, Vancouver New Music Festival, CBC Radio, La Jolla Summerfest, Scotia Festival, Montreal New Music Festival, Cervantino Festival in Mexico, and the National Concert Hall and Theater in Taipei. Born in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, Aiyun holds a DMA degree from UC San Diego. Between 2006 and 2017, she led the percussion program at McGill University and held the position of William Dawson Scholar. She currently holds the position of Professor of Music at the Faculty of Music, University of Toronto where she heads the percussion area and directs the University of Toronto Percussion Ensemble as well as the Technology and Performance Integration Research (TaPIR) Lab. She was named Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 2024.

events.title: Fall Workshop Performance: "Boy" by Anna Ziegler
events.description:
The Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies (TDPS) presents workshop performances of Boy by Anna Ziegler and directed by Mathew Chipman.
Showtimes:December 3rd at 8:00pm December 4th at 8:00pm About the Play: What happens when we decide we know another person better than they know themselves? Inspired by a true story, Boy follows the life and relationships of Adam, whose family chose to raise him as a girl following an early medical accident–as advised by his doctor. Boy is a play built around the freedom to create one's identity, the dynamics of control within relationships, and the consequences of choices one was never allowed to make. About TDPS Workshops: Workshops are designed as "capstone experiences" for advanced students in the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies (TDPS). As performance laboratories, workshops provide opportunities for student directors, choreographers, writers, and performers to develop ideas and put them into practice. Performances focus on engaging language and staging with minimal technical/design elements.

events.title: Intro to Nature Journaling for Garden Enthusiasts
events.description:
Observe the living world with curiosity and attention, and celebrate wonder in a lyric blend of science and art with a Nature Journal! Bring your love of gardens to a whole new level with a nature journal. Nature journaling is the act of putting pen (or pencil) to paper to observe aspects of nature with curiosity and attention. At this in-person workshop you'll learn about establishing (or enhancing) your nature journaling practice in the beautiful environment of the UC Botanical Garden. The focus is on experiencing and visually expressing our curiosity about plants and nature, not about making detailed botanical or wildlife art. In this practice, "art" is the experience you have while you're doing it. After a brief orientation and warm-up learning activities, you will have hands-on observation and drawing time in the Garden. Using words, pictures, and numbers you will capture the forms, shapes, and textures of the plants of your choice. You will practice foundational techniques such as basic sketching, annotation, and a variety of observational prompts that reveal deeper questions and a deeper connections to the plants. Kate will be available for questions and individual instruction during the Garden journaling time. The group will reconvene toward the close of the workshop to talk about our experiences, share work, and learn from each other. These basic materials will be provided: simple sketchbook, mechanical pencil, grey marker, and Zebra black ink brush pen. Additional specialized tools* will be provided for your use during the session. * A full take-home kit of the specialized tools will be available for purchase onsite for $15 (cash or Venmo): hardbound journal, magnifying loupe, compact mirror, clear ruler, and carry satchel/apron. * Participants are encouraged to bring any additional tools and materials that they like to use for sketching or field journaling: sketchbook, pencils, pens, measuring tools.
All skill levels welcome; no prior experience necessary. Consider adding on the afternoon workshop, Expressing Color in your Nature Journal (https://botanicalgarden.berkeley.edu/event/expressing-color-in-your-nature-journal/). The workshop will be held rain or shine. Come enjoy the beautiful botanical garden setting! This program is in both indoor and outdoor spaces.
Please reach out to gardenprograms@berkeley.edu for accessibility inquiries. Instructor Biography:Kate Rutter is an avid nature journaler, urban naturalist, educator, and native plant enthusiast who enlivens nature-human connection through sketching, observation, and curiosity. A lifelong sketcher, Kate leads nature journal workshops at public gardens, national and state parks, organizations, and nurseries. She is the author/illustrator of Bay Area Botanical and the co-creator of the Quickstart Guide to Nature Journaling. Kate holds a B.A. in Studio Art from Wellesley College and serves on the board of the Wild Wonder Foundation.

events.title: Expressing Color in your Nature Journal
events.description:
The living world is awash with color, yes, even in December! Bring your Nature Journal observations alive and learn multiple ways that color can enhance and expand your nature connection practice. Nature journaling is the act of putting pen (or pencil) to paper to observe aspects of nature with curiosity and attention; adding color brings even more life and energy to your observations. At this in-person workshop you'll learn different ways to use color (color pencils and watercolor) to deepen your observations and to accurately document nature's hues. These approaches support both art-making and field-noting skills. After a brief hands-on intro to color theory and color mixing, you'll use watercolors and/or colored pencils to use color in a variety of ways: basic color, matched color and swatches, symbolic color for diagrams and maps, and compositional color for layout and page organization. Some basic watercolor and pencil techniques will be addressed, but the focus of this session is specific to using color in a field and nature journaling setting. We wrap with a closing circle for sharing and discussion of next steps for your practice. Prior nature journaling or drawing/painting experience helpful, but not required. – These materials will be provided: set of colored pencils, sampler set of watercolors, waterbrush. – Participants please bring: a pencil (mechanical, #2 or HB pencil); a black pen with waterproof or water-resistant ink; a grey pencil or grey marker; a sketchbook suitable for working outdoors and with paper that can take some water media without bleeding through (some buckling is okay.) You're encouraged to bring any additional tools and materials that you like to use for sketching or field journaling: sketchbook, pencils, pens, measuring tools. – If you wish, you can get a kit of nature journaling supplies, available for purchase onsite for $20 (cash or Venmo). Kit includes: small softbound journal, hardbound journal, mechanical pencil, black brush pen, grey marker, magnifying loupe, compact mirror, clear ruler, and carry satchel/apron.
All skill levels welcome; no prior experience necessary. Can be taken as a stand-alone workshop, or as a follow-up to the morning workshop, Intro to Nature Journaling for Garden Enthusiasts. (https://botanicalgarden.berkeley.edu/event/intro-to-nature-journaling-for-garden-enthusiasts/) The workshop will be held rain or shine. Come enjoy the beautiful botanical garden setting! This program is held indoors.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description:
On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.
Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: On counterexamples to the unification of $\chi$ and $\chi^*$
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: David Jekel, University of OttawaOpen AI recently generated the first examples with $-\infty \chi \chi ^*$. I will contextualize and give a detailed proof of similar example, and more explicitly show the separation between free Fisher information and the large-n limit of classical Fisher information. The upper bound on free Fisher information comes from a cumulant-bound for Fisher information that draws on higher-order conjugate variable/Stein kernel techniques from classical and free settings. The lower bound on classical Fisher information comes from volume bounds on the space of matrices admitting a noticeable block structure with respect to some projections reminiscent of the volume arguments in Voiculescu's paper on absence of Cartan algebras and many subsequent works. I will derive the upper bound using a sup-formula and showing the relationship with my study of model theory and Wasserstein distance in the context of random matrices.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Boundary Control of Quantization and Emission in Photonic-Crystal Lasers
events.description: Semiconductor lasers are essential components of modern optical communication, sensing, and photonic technologies. Despite decades of progress, achieving scalable laser operation while maintaining precise control over optical properties remains an important scientific and technological challenge. Photonic crystals provide a versatile platform for investigating light-matter interactions and developing new approaches to semiconductor laser design. This dissertation investigates the fundamental properties of optical resonances and wavefunctions in finite photonic-crystal systems. Through theoretical modeling, numerical analysis, and experimental investigations, it examines the interplay between photonic band structures, cavity geometry, boundary conditions, and optical confinement. Particular attention is given to understanding how finite-size effects influence the formation and characteristics of resonant optical states. The research explores unconventional modal phenomena in photonic-crystal cavities and their implications for semiconductor laser operation. It also examines the relationship between cavity properties and optical emission, including the behavior of extended resonant states and their relevance to scalable laser architectures. These investigations provide insights into the fundamental physics of finite photonic systems and their potential applications in advanced photonic technologies. Overall, this dissertation contributes to the theoretical and experimental understanding of photonic-crystal resonances and semiconductor lasers. The findings establish a foundation for future investigations of optical confinement, cavity modes, and scalable photonic devices.

events.title: Peng Huang: "Rethinking Population Sorting in America's Political Geography"
events.description:
Abstract: Sorting, people settling into places that align with their characteristics through selective movement, is a well-documented pattern in migration studies and a central mechanism of segregation. Taking partisan sorting in the United States as an example, the talk revisits this classic topic and distinguishes two sorting processes that are often conflated. I introduce a formal definition of sorting that jointly enumerates migrants' characteristics and their alignment with both the place of origin and the destination. This exercise reveals two distinct types of sorting: attainment, in which the misaligned seek alignment, and maintenance, in which the aligned avoid losing it. I then contrast the two types through three propositions about their population base, destination accessibility, and preference structure. Statistical and simulation analyses of linked voter registration data show that maintenance sorting, though less visible, is a stronger force than attainment sorting in sustaining partisan segregation. The talk concludes by reflecting on implications for theory and methods in the study of migration, segregation, and population change.
Bio: Peng Huang is an Assistant Professor of Sociology at the University of Georgia, affiliated with the Owens Institute for Behavioral Research and the Center for the Ecology of Infectious Diseases. He develops and applies formal and computational methods to understand the interplay between population, space, and society. He studies the social and political dynamics of migration, immobility, and immigrant reception, as well as the spatial patterns and network mechanisms that shape disease diffusion and population health. Recognized with awards from sections of the American Sociological Association and the International Network for Social Network Analysis, he has work published or forthcoming in the American Sociological Review, Demography, and PNAS.

events.title: Soft Separation for Adaptive Robust Optimization (Ruiwei Jiang, University of Michigan)
events.description:
Talk title: Soft Separation for Adaptive Robust OptimizationAbstract: Adaptive Robust Optimization (ARO) finds a wide range of applications including, for example, electric power systems, supply chains, and transportation. Unfortunately, ARO models are NP-hard in general, and practical applications of ARO often resort to decision rules for tractability but sacrifice accuracy. In this talk, we propose a novel algorithmic framework for solving ARO with performance guarantees in both tractability and accuracy. The framework introduces soft separation, a probabilistic mechanism for identifying worst-case uncertainty realizations. As opposed to solving an exact separation problem iteratively, which is intractable in general, soft separation carries adversarial information forward, co-evolves with the optimization iterates, and recovers exact separation at terminal iterates with high probability. When the first-stage (here-and-now) decisions are continuous, we design a first-order method that uses soft separation to produce adaptive gradient estimates. Accordingly, we prove polynomial convergence to a surrogate that approximates the true optimum to any prescribed accuracy. When the first-stage decisions are mixed-integer, we embed soft separation in a branch-and-cut framework to generate valid cuts for the robust objective and obtain a high-probability final optimality certificate. Numerical experiments show strong performance against state-of-the-art methods, especially under scenario-based uncertainty.
Bio: Ruiwei Jiang is an Associate Professor of Industrial and Operations Engineering at the University of Michigan. His research and teaching interests lie in stochastic and integer optimization, with applications in power systems and healthcare operations. Recognitions of his work include an NSF CAREER Award, two INFORMS Junior Faculty Interest Group paper awards (1st place and honorable mention), an INFORMS Computing Society prize (honorable mention), and an IISE Operations Research Division Teaching Award.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Bridges between Hardness of Approximation and Parameterized Complexity
events.description: Approximation and parameterization are two standard ways to cope with NP-hardness. Their intersection leads to the theory of parameterized approximation: when exact fixed-parameter algorithms are unlikely, can one still obtain substantially better approximation guarantees in time f(k)n^{O(1)}? In the field of parameterized hardness of approximation, the lack of a general PCP-like theorem leaves much of the landscape unclear. We present PCP-free inapproximability for problems like k-Clique, k-SetCover and k-MDP. We also discuss progress and remaining obstacles toward a universal PCP-like theorem in the parameterized setting.

events.title: "Time and Transfiguration in Eleventh-Century Nubian Painting" by Ravinder Binning
events.description:
"Time and Transfiguration in Eleventh-Century Nubian Painting" by Ravinder Binning Abstract: Connecting Mediterranean, Nilotic, and Saharan worlds, Makurian Nubia (present-day Sudan) was one of medieval Africa's most powerful kingdoms. For over six centuries, this kingdom controlled the Middle Nile Valley and converted an older cultic landscape into a sacred Christian topography. That topography, however, was flooded during the Cold War construction of the Aswan High Dam, when many crucial Nubian monuments were lost. Medieval Nubian art survives in fragment and remains marginalized by art history. Confronting this condition, this talk examines the strategies through which eleventh-century Nubian painters framed the history of their own sacred spaces. It focuses specifically on how painters transfigured Nubian elites in mystical tableaux. The painterly evocation of fiery surfaces, luminous textiles, rushing forms, and incorruptible stones led beholders into kinesthetic encounters with multiple layers of history. Texts from the same period attest to a broader cultural inquiry into the type of visionary experience which these paintings stage.
Bio: Ravinder Binning (PhD, Stanford University) is Assistant Professor of Medieval Art History at Southern Methodist University. The principal arenas of his research and teaching are medieval western Europe, the Mediterranean world and Northeast Africa. His first book, The Medieval Art of Fear (The University of Chicago Press, 2026) tracks the development of a Christian aesthetics of fear from late antique Egypt and Jerusalem to western Europe and postmedieval colonial spaces. He is at work on a second book, Luminous Fragments: Painting and History in Medieval Nubia. Focusing on the now-lost Faras Cathedral in Sudanese Nubia, the book confronts how monumental painting in a medieval African kingdom became a medium of temporal orientation. On this and similar topics, Binning was the primary organizer of the 2023 conference at the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florence, Medieval Nubia in a Transcultural Horizon. Prior to SMU, Binning held teaching positions at Colgate University and the Ohio State University. His research has been supported by fellowships from Dumbarton Oaks, the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florence, and the Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts at the National Gallery of Art. If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact the History of Art Department at art_history@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: An attempt towards the Autistic Image feat. Perwana Nazif
events.description: A History & Theory of New Media lecture with Perwana Nazif Visiting Faculty, California Institute of the Arts, and Artistic Director, Los Angeles Review of Books - Monday, December 7, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfCVu9yc8DDE25JwxXsk8JBXMFwmawFEoFCQw71XrKximqkdQ/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MGxuYnJuZWpqNGd2ZGo1MGppNXRzMmVyM2UgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - It's here that the two attempts—allowing autistic children to exist and camering— have a trait in common: to evade intention, which requires a strange rigour that can't be intentional. "Miscreating" (1979) Just as tracing is not drawing, camering is not filming. "Miscreating" (1979) An attempt lays itself bare—and you can certainly hear all the connotations of that word. It does not present itself as a request. Le Croire et le Craindre (1978) In 1968, French educator and writer Fernand Deligny began the "Cévennes network," also known as the attempt. The Cévennes attempt was an informal, non-clinical collective of autistic children and (non-autistic) "close presences," who together enabled autistic existence. The Cévennes experiment attempted to work within a non-verbal and non-institutional framework, to respond to what Deligny marked as the autistic children's needs to experience life in the absence of language and neurotypical relation. The network both followed and radically departed from Deligny's prior para-clinical and social work with neurodivergent, psychotic, "troubled" or "delinquent," children, many of whom would have otherwise been incarcerated or permanently institutionalized. Here, in the attempt, they experimented with collective aesthetic and/or media practices outside of language: purposeless objects and common actions, non-representational cartography, tracing (unlike drawing), and camering (unlike filming). So, what or how is the collective attempt—when its conditions of emergence are indeterminacy, precarity, non-relation, and detours from if not a total outside to language and the subject? To hazard a presentation of the (Cévennes) attempt is to present it through what Deligny calls the autistic image—that which means nothing, says nothing, or does anything. This talk, then, will explore the apparatus of the autistic image, its point of seeing, and what it enables to come into the world. About Perwana Nazif Perwana Nazif teaches at the California Institute of the Arts and serves as the artistic director of the Los Angeles Review of Books. She recently edited Everybody Wants to Be a Fascist: Institutional Psychotherapy as a Resistance Movement (semiotext(e), 2025) and is a contributing editor at Parapraxis Magazine. She recently curated François Pain, Psychiatry is what Psychiatrists do at JOAN, Los Angeles and is currently working on an exhibition at CAC Brétigny in France. About History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series The History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series brings to campus leading humanities scholars working on issues of media transition and technological emergence. The series promotes new, interdisciplinary approaches to questions about the uses, meanings, causes, and effects of rapid or dramatic shifts in techno-infrastructure, information management, and forms of mediated expression. Presented by BCNM, these events are free and open to the public.
