events.title: Research & Writing in the Age of AI: Legal and Practical Considerations
events.description:
RSVP to get the Zoom linkThis workshop will help you navigate the legal and practical questions that AI tools raise for academic authors.
The first part of the session will explore how using AI tools in research implicates a range of legal issues that researchers—and the libraries that support them—need to navigate. We'll examine whether feeding content into AI tools qualifies as fair use under copyright law, and how overarching contracts such as library e-resource agreements or a website's terms of use may restrict, shape, or even override your fair use rights. We'll explore whether those clickthrough or browsewrap terms of use are enforceable, and why you may need to pay closer attention to them than you think.
The second part of the session will cover how using AI in your writing can affect your copyright and authorship, what current publisher and journal policies require you to disclose, and how AI training on scholarly work intersects with your rights as an author.
You'll leave with a working understanding of where the law currently stands, what remains unsettled, and how to make informed choices about using these tools in your own work.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Creativity Supportive Ecosystems
events.description: I think it's a good thing when people make art. How can we help communities make art more often? Creativity Support Tools (CSTs) have made the creation of content (images, music, film) faster and easier than ever... but creation technology often fails to address (or even exacerbates) major issues threatening artistic livelihoods and communities. Communities share art online at the mercy of mysterious media recommendation algorithms, on platforms crowded with slop, at the risk of nonconsensual reuse (i.e., for AI training data.) How might we reimagine the role of CSTs, and technology at large, in the face of these wicked artistic support problems? I'll present Creativity Supportive Ecosystems, a framework for understanding how creation systems interdepend on systems of distribution, reception, and provenance. I'll discuss how this ecosystemic lens grounds a perspective on designing creativity supportive infrastructure, and share Artographer, a system we built to explore using spatial-maps to research and support curation and engagement with art collections. Throughout, I'll emphasize my aggressive optimism that, not only can we use data and "AI" to support creativity & culture in new, powerful ways… we can (and should) do so while moving smaller, slower, with intention and care for community, heritage, and culture.

events.title: Multimodal Transportation Impact Analysis: California Best Practices
events.description: Description The multi-modal Transportation Impact Study (TIS) is one of the most effective tools for assessing the impacts of new land development (or redevelopment) and establishing a nexus with project mitigations, including impact fees. Recent legislation as well as public sentiment have made it imperative that transportation professionals better understand how to prepare and review these studies. Although current California environmental regulations (CEQA) require specific methods for use in analyzing transportation impacts, focusing on vehicle-miles traveled, this class will consider a broader variety of transportation impacts. A good TIS can consider a much wider range of impacts than CEQA and therefore can better reflect local community values. The class will consider such topics as site access and off-site improvements to satisfactorily accommodate project traffic, including traffic signals. It also considers how impact fees can be applied consistent with California law to recover costs associated with the new development. It also considers non-VMT impacts, such as multi-modal impacts, delay to buses, providing the right amount of parking, internal circulation, and improving the pedestrian/ bicycle environment. This 8-hour course (in 4 two-hour modules) provides the basics and practical applications of analysis procedures for determining impacts using various performance metrics on all modes (pedestrian, bicycle, transit, and auto). It emphasizes the best practices that are being employed in California and other areas. This course focuses on urban/suburban streets (non-freeways), internal circulation planning, and providing just the right amount of parking. Applications of analyses include improving transportation impact studies, environmental impact reports (EIRs) and project mitigation, new development design standards, and the CEQA review process. Attendees will also become familiar with:Labor-saving shortcuts for data collection (because some multimodal level of service methodologies can be very "data hungry") How 'induced travel demand' is defined, and when it does (or does not) create a significant environmental impact under the law Cross-modal impacts (when capacity or physical characteristics of one mode are changed and thereby affect another mode using the street) How to assess "fair share" impact fees to pay for project mitigations How parking can be used as an effective demand-management measure Available resources (web and paper) that provide further guidance This class has been updated to reflect many changes in California law between 2020 and 2024. Updates to important references-such as the 2023 Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, and ITE Recommended Practice on TIA-will also be considered. This course is a combination of instructor presentations with interactive engagements to apply the techniques in the real-world, with case studies and applications of the material. The material complements TE-43 (Multimodal Transportation Operations: Evaluation Methods & Performance Measures) (https://registration.techtransfer.berkeley.edu/CourseStatus.awp?&course=0500TE430000), and TE-60 (VMT Metrics Policy Applications and Technical Analysis for SB 743 Compliance) (https://registration.techtransfer.berkeley.edu/CourseStatus.awp?&course=0500TE600000), although each can be taken as a stand-alone class. Topics IncludeLevel-of-Service (LOS) concept– what it means and why do it, pros and cons of different methods cross-modal impacts how to calculate VMT from a proposed project gathering field information & data collection shortcuts software available to assist in analysis California statutory requirements (especially CEQA and SB 743) relationship to the latest Caltrans' guidance applications to Context Sensitive Design assessing safety impacts of projects relationship to Sustainable Transportation Indicators incorporation as part of project mitigation typical schedule and budgetary requirements increasing transit as a share of regional VMT applying analytical and simulation tools to multi-modal impact analysis What You Will Learn Students will learn how to prepare– and review– a comprehensive multi-modal transportation impact study. This includes studies prepared both to support CEQA documentation as well as stand-alone studies. Topics include basic level-of-service (LOS) concepts for all modes, and how to apply them to conduct performance and level-of-service analysis for various types of urban streets with various levels of accommodation for different modes; determine the impacts of system improvements using vehicle miles traveled (VMT); and analyze operational impacts of possible changes in the allocation of street cross-section to various modes. Who Should Attend Planners, engineers, technicians, and others at all levels of experience, who prepare or review transportation impacts from land developments will benefit from this class. A minimal level of mathematics is required (basic algebra). Requirements Participants will need a basic calculator for several in-class problem sets. A complete PDF set of Course Notes will be provided by the instructors.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1

events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Marvin Parasram, Associate Professor,New York UniversityThe Photochemistry of Nitro Compounds for Carbon-Carbon and Carbon-Heteroatom Bond Formation Nitro-containing compounds, such as nitroarenes and nitroalkanes, are featured in materials and pharmaceuticals and are versatile compounds in organic chemistry. While critical intermediates in synthesis, the photoreactivity of nitro-containing compounds has been less studied. Our laboratory has found that photoexcited nitroarenes can serve as both the hydrocarbon activator and the heteroatom source to enable economical C–H hydroxylation reactions. We have also found that photoexcited nitroarenes can serve as anaerobic oxygen-atom transfer agents, leading to valuable carbonyl derivatives via anaerobic cleavage of alkenes, a practical alternative to ozonolysis. Recently, we have demonstrated a photoinduced cross-denitrative olefination of nitroalkanes to afford synthetically valuable tri- and tetrasubstituted alkenes. Mechanistic studies reveal a photoinitiated, photopropagated nucleophilic-radical substitution and radical-chain elimination sequence in which in situ nitronates function as photoreductants to generate radical-anion intermediates that undergo subsequent photo-driven β-elimination. These findings demonstrate the synthetic utility of photoexcited nitro compounds to enable useful C–C and C–heteroatom bond-forming events.

events.title: Jitendra Malik: Science of Intelligence
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Wednesday, December 9, 2026 Time: 12:00pm Location: 101 Weill Hall Speaker: Jitendra Malik (https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=aOklxsQAAAAJ&hl=en) Affiliation: UC Berkeley EECS (https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~malik/)

events.description: UC Berkeley students, faculty, and staff are warmly invited to join a Campus Conversation about justice and peace in Palestine and Israel with Aziz Abu Sarah and Maoz Inon, Palestinian and Israeli peace activists and co-authors of NYTimes Bestseller, The Future Is Peace, Wednesday, Dec 9th, 12:30 - 2:30pm. Register here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/19GSclpCH6eBCmyhqO0YTrKJL1umJq3GMmC-4rZhHS_8/edit) and receive the event location. Abu Sarah and Inon have experienced tremendous personal losses and have chosen to dedicate their lives to the pursuit of justice and peace. They have given talks across the globe, and addressed members of the European Parliament, members of congress (https://www.americanprogress.org/events/peace-is-possible-an-alternative-vision-for-israel-and-palestine/), and met at the Vatican with Pope Leo. They have been interviewed on The Daily Show by Jon Stewart (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DU45iLNBwro); and their Ted Talk (https://www.ted.com/talks/aziz_abu_sarah_and_maoz_inon_a_palestinian_and_an_israeli_face_to_face) was the third most watched in 2024. Their radical and hopeful efforts come against the backdrop of the violence of October 7, 2023, the destruction of Gaza, the increasing violence in the West Bank, and the wars in the region more broadly, which have caused immense grief, anger, and despair worldwide, and have deeply divided many on our campus. Many of us feel trapped under the extraordinary weight of the tremendous suffering we see daily through images on the news and social media, and yet we often lack the space or capacity to discuss our pain with one another, to seek out the experiences of others, or to feel seen and understood. These activists embody the possibility of empathy and connection even in the face of immense suffering, and they model what it looks like to do so without equating pain or power. This Campus Conversation will be a courageous space for all Berkeley students, faculty, and staff to bring their truths, encounter others', and learn. events.title: Jennifer Lippincott-Schwartz: Harnessing mRNA to Illuminate the Hidden World of Cells
events.description:
Advances in mRNA-based imaging technologies are enabling unprecedented views of cellular architecture and dynamics. This talk will present two stories that employ synthetic mRNA to probe the spatial and temporal organization of living cells. First, I will describe a generalizable system for in vitro-transcribed (IVT) mRNAs, optimized for high translational efficiency across multiple cell types while reducing stress pathway activation. This platform, termed mRNAbow, supports simultaneous expression of multiple fluorescent proteins, enabling multiplexed imaging in mammalian cells-including cancer lines, iPSC-derived models, primary cells, and organoids-as well as in vivo contexts such as zebrafish embryos. In a different application, MS2 and SUNTAG-based live-cell reporters were used to visualize mRNA dynamics and translation at single-molecule resolution. We find that translation of mRNAs encoding membrane and secretory proteins is enriched at endoplasmic reticulum (ER) junctions containing the structural protein lunapark and localized adjacent to lysosomes. These results reveal a coupling between ER organization, lysosomal nutrient sensing, and the localized synthesis of secretory and membrane proteins, linking spatial cell architecture to translational control.
Division(s): Divisions of Biochemistry, Biophysics & Structural Biology, Division of Cell Biology, Development & Physiology, and Genetics, Genomics, Evolution & Development

events.title: San Francisco & Silicon Valley Alumni: Reinventing Success: Building a Fulfilling Career Transition
events.location: Silkroad Innovation Hub, 724 Oak Grove Ave #100, Menlo Park, CA 94025, USA
events.description:
For many accomplished professionals, the hardest career question comes after achieving what they once worked toward: what happens when the traditional definition of success no longer feels aligned?

Join the Berkeley Haas Alumni Network for an intimate fireside conversation with Regina Sih-Meynier, Pharm.D., former pharmaceutical leader, entrepreneur, advisor to Berkeley SkyDeck startups, and award-winning author of A Thousand Whispers from Within: Manifesting a Life of Purpose and Prosperity. Drawing on her own journey from a two-decade corporate career into entrepreneurship and purpose-driven work, and on her experience coaching, Regina will explore how experienced professionals can navigate major transitions, rethink what success means, and develop the mindset, energy, and resilience required to build what comes next.

​This is not a conversation about simply finding the next job. It is about building the next chapter, and fulfilling/sustaining yourself while you do it.

​Topics include:

​Recognizing When It’s Time for Change: Distinguishing between a difficult season and a genuine need for change. Untangling your identity from your career, title, status, or achievements.

​Navigating the Decision and Transition: Making consequential decisions when analysis alone can’t provide the answer. Navigating uncertainty and setbacks without losing momentum. Protecting your energy, focus, and resilience during periods of change.

​Designing the Next Chapter: Redefining success without discarding everything you’ve already built. Turning decades of experience, relationships, and credibility into an advantage. Exploring a next chapter that may span entrepreneurship, advising, investing, board service, teaching, or writing.

​Whether you are actively navigating a transition, considering entrepreneurship or a portfolio career, or simply asking what you want the next phase of your professional life to look like, this conversation will offer practical insight into both the external decisions and the internal mindset required to make reinvention sustainable.

Questions? Contact Zhanara Amans – amanszh@gmail.com .

events.title: Danette Daniels: Towards new cancer medicines with degraders of chromatin regulatory proteins
events.description:
Targeted protein degradation as a therapeutic modality has experienced an explosion in research the past several years resulting in advancements of numerous degraders to the clinic addressing a wide variety of disease indications. The strengths of this induced proximity modality include its catalytic mechanism, the ability to drug non-enzymatic targets which serve as scaffolds, and introduction of selectivity amongst paralog family members. In this talk, we will highlight our work developing highly selective and potent degraders to CREB binding protein (CBP), E1A binding protein (EP300), and a historically intractable target, ARID1B. Each of these targets regulate a myriad of cellular processes and have been implicated in numerous oncology diseases. CBP and EP300 are two paralog histone acetyltransferases and while several classes of inhibitors have been developed to CBP/EP300, they have dual activity leading to tolerability challenges. Meanwhile, ARID1B, a core component of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, has long been considered undruggable due to the absence of known binders and lack of ligandable pockets. Striking dependency on ARID1B is observed across multiple cancer indications harboring ARID1A mutations, highlighting a synthetic lethal relationship between these paralogs. In this talk I will highlight the mechanisms for which enabled development of binders and subsequently selective degraders to each other these targets. With these selective compounds in hand, we then demonstrate strong anti-proliferative effects and for CBP and EP300, in vivo tumor growth inhibition across numerous oncology indications with an improved therapeutic window as compared to dual inhibition.
Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection (copy)
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.
Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. events.title: OEW Seminar - Leah Boustan (Yale)
events.description: Topic: "The Immigrant Advantage in US Intergenerational Mobility" Abstract: Why do children of immigrants experience greater upward mobility than children of US-born parents? We construct parent-child linked data from federal tax returns, household surveys and Social Security Administration records. Immigrant parents from all sending regions are positively selected, ranking higher in the educational distributions of their countries of origin than US-born parents with similar incomes. This parental advantage shapes parenting practices and investments in children. For most children of immigrants, higher parental education rank is associated with greater college attendance, particularly at selective institutions and in STEM fields. For children of Latin American immigrants, higher parental educational rank is instead associated with stronger labor force attachment. Unlike in the early twentieth century, immigrant families do not settle in more economically advantaged locations.

events.title: "Looking Again at the St. Albans Psalter: Trans Media, Imaginary Queerness, and the 'Real' Middle Ages" by Christopher T. Richards
events.description: "Looking Again at the St. Albans Psalter: Trans Media, Imaginary Queerness, and the 'Real' Middle Ages" by Christopher T. RichardsAbstract: Contemporary discourse often casts queer and trans lives as imaginary: unreal, artificial, and detached from the realities of the body and history. In the Middle Ages, however, trans embodiment could model the imaginative work of artistic creation. This paper revisits the twelfth-century St. Albans Psalter through the intertwined histories of medieval painting and gender. Made and remade over decades, the Psalter is a composite object whose additions, removals, and rearrangements have challenged codicological and art-historical interpretation. To account for the book's unusual qualities, scholars often invoke its probable owner Christina of Markyate, yet scholars have circumscribed Christina's agency in the book's making, treating her status as a woman as incompatible with artistic authority. Focusing on a historiated initial, I reconsider a bearded, haloed figure whose gesture corresponds to an episode in Christina's Vita, where they cross-dress becoming "a manly soldier of God." I turn to the Vita's vocabulary of sculpting, painting, and remaking to connect Christina's multiple gender transformations with the Psalter's material transformations. I argue that the manuscript invites us to understand illumination as a trans medium, through which the self can be imagined otherwise and making is always remaking, or raluminer in the Psalter's Old French. By reclaiming the imaginary as a space of artistic and gendered possibility, the Psalter also challenges modern assumptions about the historical reality of trans life. Looking again at this canonical medieval artwork, I suggest, means looking again at what we understand the Middle Ages—and the real—to have been. Bio:Christopher T. Richards is a medieval art historian whose research explores the intersections of image theory and the history of sexuality, with particular attention to queer and psychoanalytic approaches to medieval visual culture. He is the Talbot-Sage Assistant Professor of Art History at the University of Alaska Anchorage. His recent essays examine late-medieval French illuminated manuscripts as sites for theorizing art and the artist, and have appeared in Art History, Arthuriana, and Different Visions, among other venues. His public-facing work, including exhibitions, podcasts, and collaborations with contemporary artists, explores how contemporary art might open new approaches to medieval and queer historiography. Richards is currently preparing two books for publication: a catalogue of the illuminated manuscripts of the Ovide moralisé, a fourteenth-century adaptation of Ovid's Metamorphoses, and a thematic study of medieval painting as a trans medium, from which his talk derives. Above all, he loves working in the classroom with students to discover the unexpected queerness of the medieval past, a world at once distant from and surprisingly intimate with our own. events.title: Film Screening: Let the Summer Never Come Again
events.description: Alexandre Koberidze in Person The opening on-screen text reads: "Love has no end—a story always has. You will now see a love story." Told in three parts through the use of voice-over and text, Let the Summer Never Come Again follows a young man who arrives in Tbilisi to audition for a dance troupe. When the audition is delayed, he gets involved in illegal activities, including sleeping with men for money, until he falls in love with a military officer. This is the first of Alexandre Koberidze's features shot on a Sony Ericsson cellphone, rendering softness in the image and saturated colors that create a kind of abstraction and offer distance from reality.

events.title: Film Screening: To Be or Not to Be
events.description: This film is a delightfully satirical comedy set in Nazi-occupied Warsaw—an obvious contradiction in terms in the hands of anyone but Ernst Lubitsch. Jack Benny, leading a troupe of ham actors in outsmarting the Gestapo by reducing them to ridicule, gives a beautifully paced, more than typically animated performance, disguised along the way as a Gestapo agent and Hamlet himself. Carole Lombard as his footsie-playing wife and fellow trouper is ingenious in what was to be her last film role. "What I have satirized in this picture," Lubitsch wrote in 1943, "are the Nazis and their ridiculous ideology." —Judy Bloch

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description:
On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.
Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.description: 4K Digital Restoration In this exquisite gem of a comedy, Herbert Marshall (Gaston) and Miriam Hopkins (Lily) are outlaw lovers—jewel thieves masquerading as European sophisticates and relishing the charade. events.title: Mathew Kiang: "Who Counts? Measurement, Models, and Inequality in US Mortality"
events.description:
Abstract: Although death reporting in the United States is essentially complete, the quality of US mortality data varies widely across both space and time. Sociodemographic information can be misclassified, and specific causes of death are often uncertain or poorly measured. Drug-specific and COVID-19 mortality are two examples. For COVID-19, researchers often turned to excess mortality estimation, partly to avoid relying on misdiagnosed or undiagnosed causes of death. However, we lack a general framework for estimating excess mortality, and it is unclear when or if some approaches are more appropriate than others. As a result, current attempts to estimate excess mortality vary dramatically in the underlying model type and associated researcher decisions. Here, I use a multiverse analysis to systematically examine a wide range of reasonable researcher decisions and empirically evaluate how these decisions impact estimates of COVID-19 excess mortality in the US. I end by asking how we count deaths, and who those counts leave out.
Bio: Mathew Kiang is an Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Population Health at Stanford University School of Medicine. A social epidemiologist and computational social scientist, he studies health inequities in the United States, with a focus on drug overdose and COVID-19 mortality. His work combines traditional health data, such as death certificates, with novel, non-health data, such as mobile phone records and online discussions. He holds an ScD from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, has served on multiple National Academies consensus committees, and received the 2026 American College of Epidemiology Early Career Epidemiologist Award.

events.title: "The Racialized Scentscape of Fatimid Automata" by Holley Ledbetter
events.description:
"The Racialized Scentscape of Fatimid Automata" by Holley LedbetterAbstract: In the early twelfth century, the Fatimid vizier al-Afal Shāhanshāh (d. 1121) reportedly adorned his private sitting room in Cairo with eight life-size automata representing enslaved women. Court historian Ibn Muyassar (d. 1278) notes that four of these mechanical sculptures were white and made from camphor, while the remaining four were black and made from ambergris. Lavishly dressed and bejeweled, the gynoids bowed in servitude upon the vizier's entrance before returning to their upright positions. Although no longer extant, their unusual combination of mechanical movement, racialized representation, and aromatic materials offers a compelling opportunity to reconsider the sensory dimensions of racialization and enslavement in the medieval Islamic world. Drawing on critical race theory, sensory studies, and medieval Arabic literary and scientific discourse, my talk examines how the Fatimid automata potentially participated in the construction and naturalization of racial difference through a multisensory aesthetics of enslavement.
Bio: Holley Ledbetter specializes in Islamic art and architecture of the caliphal period (c. 650-1250) in Egypt, the Levant, and around the Mediterranean Basin, with a particular focus on mechanical devices, representations of enslaved populations, and the intersection of race and gender. She earned her PhD in the History of Art from the University of Michigan in 2026. Her first book project, tentatively titled The Visual Poetics of Wonder in the Fatimid World, argues that the Fatimid court cultivated an aesthetics of wonder to legitimize caliphal authority through objects that embodied rhetorical devices drawn from Classical Arabic literary theory. She also pursues research on censorship and iconoclasm in the contemporary Arab world and is co-editing Visual Triggers: Image-Based Battles in Today's Public Sphere, a volume that includes her essay on the widespread dissemination and subsequent censorship of Palestinian images of defiance from Gaza. events.title: Tuning In Together: Using Music to Navigate Caregiving
events.description: This workshop explores the healing potential of music for both caregivers and their loved ones. Drawing from neuroscience, psychology, and lived clinical experience, psychologist and musician Barbara Minton will discuss how music affects the brain, supports emotional regulation, reduces stress, enhances connection, and can create moments of presence and meaning even in the midst of caregiving demands. She will be joined by her colleague, Peppino D'Agostino, a virtuosic guitarist, who will perform live music from their collaborative work in which they create compositions designed to support nervous system regulation and emotional well-being. Participants will leave with practical insights and simple music-based tools to support resilience, connection, and well-being in everyday life. Presenter: Dr. Barbara Minton, Phd Dr. Minton earned her BA in Psychology, summa cum laude, from the University of Denver, followed by PhDs in Psychology with an emphasis in developmental and child clinical practice. Demonstrating her deep commitment to brain science, she is Board Certified in Neurofeedback and holds the distinction of Diplomate in Quantitative Electroencephalogram (QEEG). Her diverse career includes private clinical practice in Boise, Idaho, serving as Mental Health Education Coordinator for the State of Alaska's Department of Health and Social Services, and as Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Alaska Southeast. These roles have allowed her to cultivate expertise not just in psychological assessment and neurofeedback, but also in the deeply human areas of giftedness and hypnotherapy. Peppino D'Agostino A native of Italy, D'Agostino has made his considerable international mark as a musical artist on the guitar since he arrived in America 40 years ago. In 2017 Guitar Player listed him as one of the 50 transcendent guitar superheroes of all times. The CD "Every Step of The Way" was awarded by Acoustic Guitar's People's Choice Awards with a Bronze medal for Best Acoustic Album of All Time. His signature Seagull acoustic guitar has been voted among the ten best signature guitars by Guitar Player magazine. Peppino gives guitar workshops, master classes and seminars worldwide. To date Peppino has recorded 19 CD's, performed in over thirty five countries at international festivals and concert halls. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.

events.title: Film Screening: Here Is Your Life
events.description: 4K Digital RestorationHere Is Your Life is one of the most auspicious debuts in Swedish cinema. Capturing the atmosphere of early twentieth-century Sweden, it is the story of a working-class boy's awakenings—political, educational, sexual. Teenager Olof (Eddie Axberg) leaves home to venture into the workforce, cycling through positions as a logger, brickmaker, and traveling film projectionist. Curious and resilient, Olof finds a life as rich in travails as it is in joys. Jan Troell's extraordinary black-and-white photography, accentuated with short, colorful reveries, creates a film that is at once realistic and lyrical.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.

events.title: Film Screening: 2001: A Space Odyssey
events.description: 4K Digital Restoration Stanley Kubrick's cinematic milestone was in every sense an experimental film, harnessing its widescreen, epic format for an intensely metaphysical, ultimately very personal use. The film was conceived less as a science fiction narrative than as an experience in space and time. As a re-creation of the dimensions of outer space, taking us beyond deep focus into infinite focus, it has never been matched—neither has the grace with which Kubrick's pristine visuals literally waltz through several millennia of evolution. The film's most memorable character, the computer HAL, is the embodiment of evolutionary anxiety as we leave the mechanical age for the digital one. —Judy Bloch, Edith Kramer

events.title: Film Screening: The Flight of the Eagle
events.description: Digital Restoration In this fictionalized account of a true story, Max von Sydow stars as Salomon August Andrée, an aeronautical engineer with the hubristic ambition to be the first man to reach the North Pole. His three-person 1897 balloon expedition, which was heralded for its "masculine power" before takeoff, was fated for failure. As director, cowriter, cinematographer, and editor, Jan Troell attends to every stage of the explorers' preparation for the journey, the verisimilitude of the period detail supplying an icy expanse for rich characterizations from the three leads. "Magnificently photographed . . . both panoramic and unusually intimate" (Vincent Canby, New York Times). —Jeff Griffith-Perham

Based extremely loosely on master [science fiction] writer Philip K. But the line between his Chandleresque alienation and the replicants' deficiencies of soul turns exceedingly thin" (Scott Simmon, Mary Pickford Theater, Library of Congress).

events.title: Film Screening: The Shop Around the Corner
events.description: Although his art is often described in terms of social satire, verbal wit, and elegant mise-en-scène, Ernst Lubitsch was himself an actor once, in love with the profession's honorable pretense. What makes the love story here so intelligent and touching is the very way in which the lovers (James Stewart and Margaret Sullavan, coworkers in a Budapest shop who don't realize that they are secret pen pals) confuse their ideal, role-playing sense of themselves with the reality. The shop is a sufficient world, full of instinctive familiarity and sublime misunderstandings; its natural comedy is all the greater in that no "comedian" is in the cast. —David Thomson

events.title: Film Screening: Brazil
events.description: 4K Digital Restoration | Director's Cut Terry Gilliam's anti-bureaucratic satire is a kaleidoscopic epic in which architecture and nightmarish indifference conspire to make an ordinary paper shuffler (the priceless Jonathan Pryce) into a victim of everyday apocalypse. The film captures a horror of building materials crowding out inhabitants (Robert De Niro is memorable as a pipe-and-duct prole), and the vertical power of the Hybrid City is given cinematic shape. The French, as usual, have a word for it—retrofuture—and architecture to match: for instance, in the self-reflexive Pompidou Centre, with its insides on the outside, or in the unintentionally nightmarish verticality of Palais d'Abraxis, an apartment complex in Marne-la-Vallée in suburban Paris, which was used extensively in the filming.

events.title: Film Screening: Sherlock Jr.
events.description: Judith Rosenberg on PianoSherlock Jr. is Buster Keaton's most enduring commentary on the cinema, the beautiful machine that has the power to make artists of us all. Keaton plays a projectionist who dreams his way onto the screen and into a movie in which he resolves the conflicts of his own life. The film is equally impressive for Keaton's brilliantly modulated acrobatics—off-screen, the hapless hero hoists himself on his own banana peel, but on-screen, he can ride on the handlebars of a driverless motorcycle, make a boat out of a car, and perform any number of cinematic miracles without special effects. —Judy Bloch

events.title: Film Screening: The Love Parade
events.description: 4K Digital Restoration Like so many Ernst Lubitsch films, the musical The Love Parade asserts that the road to romance is paved with cynicism, of which women are the chief bearers. Maurice Chevalier marries Jeanette MacDonald, ruler of a feminist queendom, and discovers his true position when the wedding ceremony pronounces them "Wife and Man." The witty plot satirizes contemporary mores as well as film/operetta conventions. Lubitsch revels in the artificiality of the musical form rather than trying to disguise it; at the same time, he manages to keep the fluidity of his silent films by using such devices as off-screen speech or conversations that take place, unheard, behind a window. —Judy Bloch

events.title: Film Screening: The Emigrants
events.description: 4K Digital Restoration The first of Jan Troell's two films adapted from epic novels by Vilhelm Moberg stars Liv Ullmann and Max von Sydow as struggling Swedish farmers in the 1840s who decide to emigrate to America. The Emigrants received Academy Award nominations for Best Picture, Actress, Director, and Adapted Screenplay—rare honors for a foreign film. Ullmann, often identified with Ingmar Bergman's films, said Kristina is her favorite role. Troell, also acting as cinematographer, "expands our notions of what screen lyricism is, because he's solemn and yet lyrical, disciplined yet rapturous" (Pauline Kael, New Yorker). —Richard Peterson

events.title: Film Screening: Metropolis
events.description: The Complete Version Fritz Lang's futuristic super-production is an anxiety dream of urban dystopia expressed as science fiction. Set in the year 2026, Metropolis envisions a repressive techno-oligarchy in which soaring Art Deco towers and overhead freeways mock an underclass of techno slaves ruled by a "supertrustee" (Alfred Abel), who lives with his collaborators in the paradisiacal nightclub of Yoshiwara. Lang even posits a virtual woman, an evil doppelgänger cloned from the people's hero and spokeswoman, Maria (Brigitte Helm), as another principal force in this exquisite ballet of machines and men. Presented in the 2010 restored complete version, with twenty-five minutes of restored footage.

events.title: Film Screening: One Hour with You
events.description: 4K Digital Restoration | Introduced by Jonathan MackrisOne Hour with You, a musical remake of Ernst Lubitsch's own The Marriage Circle and a Best Picture Oscar nominee in 1932, stars Maurice Chevalier and Jeanette MacDonald as the happily married—shockingly so—Parisian couple whose inevitable infidelities seem forced upon them by the rapacious flirtations of Genevieve Tobin. Utilizing Chevalier's frequent asides to the audience ("What would you do?"), One Hour with You is more direct in its leering innuendo than any other Lubitsch comedy of the 1930s. With a procession of double entendres, hidden meanings, mistaken assumptions, and off-camera assignations, the film is a virtual catalog of the stylistic devices used by Lubitsch throughout his career. The final scene, with its relay of looks and pantomimed promptings, is one of the most delightful in the director's oeuvre.

The film captures a horror of building materials crowding out inhabitants (Robert De Niro is memorable as a pipe-and-duct prole), and the vertical power of the Hybrid City is given cinematic shape. events.description: 4K Digital Restoration "Together, The Emigrants and The New Land offer the pleasures of a big novel with a solid spine" (Pauline Kael, New Yorker). events.title: Antonia Mardones Marshall | Unsettling Whiteness: Race, Nation, and Afro-Descendant Recognition in Argentina and Chile
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.location: 2334 Bowditch St., Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description:
Event Description Argentina and Chile have long imagined themselves as predominantly white nations, marginalizing the presence and histories of African-descended populations from dominant narratives of national identity. Yet over the past several decades, Afro-descendant activists in both countries have challenged these narratives and successfully pressed states to recognize Black populations that were long rendered invisible. Drawing on ethnographic research, interviews, and archival and documentary sources, this talk examines the political struggles through which Afro-descendant recognition emerged in Argentina and Chile and what these processes reveal about the making and remaking of racial categories. Situating contemporary mobilization within longer histories of nation-building, racial classification, migration, and state projects of whiteness, Mardones Marshall shows how racial categories are produced through interactions among social movements, state institutions, and transnational actors. The comparison also reveals why similar demands for recognition can produce different political possibilities across national and local contexts.
Speaker Antonia Mardones Marshall is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Education at the Universidad de Tarapacá in Arica, Chile, and a Principal Investigator at the Millennium Nucleus on Perceptions and Consequences of Immigration (MIGRA). She received her Ph.D. in Sociology from UC Berkeley in 2024 and is currently a Luksic Visiting Scholar at Stanford University's Center for Latin American Studies. Her research examines race and ethnicity, migration, national identity, and the politics of classification and recognition in Latin America. Her current book, Unsettling Whiteness: The Struggle for Afro-Descendant Recognition in Argentina and Chile, is under advance contract with Stanford University Press.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
Tim Su, Assistant Professor, UC RiversideTitle: Main Group Molecular ElectronicsThis talk will describe our program to explore the synthesis and quantum transport properties of main group molecular electronics. The field of single-molecule electronics is primarily built upon charge transport studies of organic molecules. The boundaries for what we think is possible in molecular electronics are thus defined by the electronic idiosyncrasies of a single element carbon. What new quantum transport phenomena may emerge if we expand our view beyond carbon? Molecular silicon wires represent an attractive gateway to expand this understanding, as silicon is structurally similar to its group 14 congener, carbon, yet possesses distinct electronics due to the increased electropositivity, orbital energy, diffuseness, and size of its atomic orbitals. Over the last several years, we have developed synthetic approaches to exquisitely tune the peripheral and core structure of Si diamondoids, molecular cutouts of crystalline silicon. This precise synthetic control has allowed us to build higher-order materials as well as wire individual clusters between electrodes to interrogate their quantum transport via the scanning tunneling microscope break-junction (STM-BJ) technique. In this endeavor, we have discovered for the first time how to dynamically control destructive σ-quantum interference (σ-DQI) in molecular junctions and how to dictate the quantity and energetic ordering of midgap transmission anti-resonances, the hallmark signatures of DQI. We are now broadening our view beyond saturated silicon toward the broader p-block to reach new frontiers in quantum electronic transport.
The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Mobility of Medical Knowledge across Eurasia under the Mongols
events.description:
The Mongol Empire facilitated the movement of people, goods, and knowledge across Eurasia, creating new opportunities for the exchange of medical traditions. This lecture explores how medical knowledge circulated under Mongol rule and how it was received, adapted, and transmitted in East Asia. Focusing on two medical texts compiled during the Yuan (The Great Khan Ulus)—the Yuyaoyuan fang (御藥院方, Formulas of the Imperial Pharmacy) and the Yinshan zhengyao (飲膳正要, Essentials of Food and Drink)—the lecture examines the compilation of medical knowledge at the Yuan court and the introduction of West Asian medicinal substances and dietary practices. It also considers how selected medical knowledge and practices were transmitted and reinterpreted in Korea during the subsequent centuries.
Won Cho is Professor of East Asian History at Pusan National University in South Korea and currently a Visiting Scholar at the Center for Chinese Studies, University of California, Berkeley. She received her Ph.D. from Peking University in 2012, with a dissertation on the Darughachi system of the Mongol Empire. In 2014, she conducted postdoctoral research at Seoul National University on the historiography of the Mongol-Yuan period in the Qing Empire. Her research has primarily focused on the institutional and legal history of the Mongol Empire, particularly Yuan China. In recent years, her research has expanded to the history of medicine, particularly the circulation and transmission of medical knowledge across Eurasia under Mongol rule.

events.title: Uncertain Futures: Immigration Law and Detention in the U.S. Today
events.description:
Featuring:

Cecillia Wang, National Legal Director, ACLU

Mary Moriarty, County Attorney, Hennepin County

…with more to come!

The Trump administration has dramatically altered the field of immigration law over the last two years. Scholars and practitioners are navigating an unclear and continuously shifting political, legal, and narrative landscape. Migrants are being made increasingly vulnerable to new and deadly regimes of immigration governance.

This timely symposium convenes scholars, immigration law practitioners, journalists, and impacted migrants to discuss challenges in the field and current legal battles to defend the rights of noncitizens. What constitutional due process rights and humanitarian protections still exist for migrants in detention? What kind of storytelling can legal practitioners and allies engage in to reaffirm the humanity of their noncitizen community members? What is at stake when immigration status is weaponized to silence dissenters? This symposium explores these consequential questions as immigration law finds itself at a crossroads.

Questions? Contact cljc@berkeley.edu .

events.title: Lecture | The Invention of the Fertile Crescent: Historical Lessons from American Orientalism
events.description:
Abstract: During five decades that spanned the turn of the twentieth century (about 1870 to 1920), a tradition of oriental scholarship took firm root in the United States. American orientalists conducted rigorous research into the history and languages of the ancient Near East. These scholars were early defenders of a modern liberal education in the United States. They invented the idea of "Western civilization" and argued that the origins of the West lay in the ancient Orient. They coined the concept of the "fertile crescent" to suggest that the lands of the Near East gently nurtured humanity in its early days, "cradling" civilization in the nascent stage. This lecture will examine American orientalism's quest to find historical, rather than biblical, origin stories for humanity. In the orientalist scheme, the civilizations of the East were the first to develop monotheistic religion and thus to foster humankind's capacity for empathy. Empathy, in turn, played an essential role in the functioning of democratic society in the modern West.
Bio: Serena Shah is a PhD candidate in U.S. History at Stanford University. She works on the history of ideas and the production of knowledge in major American cultural institutions, especially universities and museums. Her dissertation examines the uses of American oriental scholarship for liberal education in the fin-de-siècle United States. Serena also broadly studies Americans' ideas about antiquity in the nineteenth century; she is in the process of publishing a research article on Greek and Roman slave-naming practices in the antebellum era. She received her A.B. (summa cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa) from Harvard University in 2021 and her M.A. in History from Stanford in 2023.

events.title: Danielle Roper | Hemispheric Blackface: A Reflection on Racial Impersonation
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description:
Event description In Hemispheric Blackface, Danielle Roper examines blackface performance and its relationship to 20th- and 21st-century nationalist fictions of mestizaje, creole nationalism, and other versions of postracialism in the Americas. Challenging both the dominance of the US minstrel tradition and the focus on the nation in blackface studies, Roper maps a hemispheric network of racial impersonation in Peru, Bolivia, Colombia, Jamaica, Cuba, and Miami. She analyzes blackface performance in the aftermath of the turn to multiculturalism in Latin America, the emergence of modern blackness in Jamaica, and the rise of Barack Obama in the United States, showing how blackface remains embedded in cultural entertainment. Contending that the Americas are linked by repeating nationalist fictions of postracialism, colorblindness, and myths of racial democracy, Roper assesses how acts of impersonation mediate the ongoing power of these narratives and enable people to comprehend advancements and reversals in racial equality. Rather than simply framing blackface as liberatory or oppressive, Roper traces its emergence from a shared history of slavery and the varied politics of racial enjoyment throughout the hemisphere. Roper will also lead a two-hour mini-seminar titled "Abject Pleasures in the Postcolonial Below: Theatre in Jamaica." The mini seminar will take place on Friday, January 29, at 9:30 am and is for Berkeley graduate students. Interested students should email clacs@berkeley.edu for consideration.
Organized by CLACS and Nadia Ellis (English). Co-sponsored by the Department of African American Studies.
SpeakerDanielle Roper is Associate Professor of Romance Languages and Literatures at the University of Chicago. She is the author of Hemispheric Blackface: Impersonation and Nationalist Fiction in the Americas (Duke University Press 2025) which was written with the support of Neubauer Family Assistant Professorship. Her work on racial impersonation, radical feminist activism, queer visual art across the Hemispheric Americas has been published in GLQ, Latin American Research Review, SmallAxe, TDR, and elsewhere. She is the curator of the digital exhibit Visualizing/Performing Blackness in the Afterlives of Slavery: A Caribbean Archive.

events.title: Neil Bartlett Memorial Lecture
events.description: Michael Hill, Professor, University of BathTitle:Not just there to balance the charge: cation identity in molecular s-blockchemistry Familiar to anybody who likes salt on their fries, a quintessential feature of alkaline metal chemistry is the stability and resistance to reduction of the group 1 and group 2 cations. In such cases, little consideration is usually given to the significant changes in reactivity that can result from the exchange of one cation for another. Similarly, almost as an article of chemical faith, the resultant M + and M 2+ oxidation states are generally considered incorruptible. This presentation will summarise the impacts of such variations on both catalytic and stoichiometric reactivity, along with our observations of how apparently superficial changes to alkaline metal identity, and even redox behaviour, can impact on our ability to synthesise s-block, p-block and d-block molecules such as those shown below.

events.description: Christian Limberg, Professor, Humboldt University of BerlinBiomimetic Thiolate Dioxygenation at Iron Centres and Bioinspired Carbonite Binding at Nickel/Iron SitesLecture 1 of 2 In the first part the generation of Ni–CO22-…M complexes (M = alkali,1-3 earth alkaline4 or transition metal ion6) via hitherto rarely observed formate β‑deprotonation is reported.1-3 The CO22- (carbonite) ligand is bound like a carbene to the nickel centre and was found to interact with the counterions M+, introduced via the used bases or salt metathesis reactions. Through their properties they thus significantly influence the stability and reactivity of the complexes, which resemble the CO2 bound state in Ni,Fe carbon monoxide dehydrogenases (CODH),5 in particular the Ni–CO22-…Fe representative.6 For the series of systems presented an inverse relation between redox behaviour and activation emerged: transition metal ions reduce the reduction potential of the carbonite unit but increase its tendency to undergo C-O bond cleavage.6 Mononuclear non-heme iron enzymes, which activate dioxygen for the subsequent oxygenation of substrates, form the background of the second part. The cysteine dioxygenase (CDO) is a representative of the (His)3Fe-enzyme family and catalyzes the reaction between cysteine and dioxygen to yield cysteine sulfinic acid, which lies at the branching point of cysteine catabolism. Understanding of the CDO may guide the way to suitable catalysts for synthetically highly interesting thiol dioxygenations and hence the development of model complexes that mimic the active sites of these enzymes is a valuable but also challenging target: iron oxidation instead of S‐oxygenation as well as overoxidation at the S atom has to be avoided.8 The lecture reflects our progress in the development of low-molecular weight analogues, were the (His)3Fe moiety is simulated by a tris(pyrazolyl)borate-iron complex metal fragment.7-12 Recent findings concerning the replacement of thiolates by selenium-based substrates are also presented.7

events.title: Domesticated: Cultivated Species and The Creation Of Networks
events.description:
Domesticated: Cultivated Species and The Creation Of Networks Over the last two decades, archaeological research across north-central Asia has led to a clarification of the timing of the introduction of domesticated animals and plants. The translocation and integration of new species marked major thresholds in human history, for example as economies in north-central Asia shifted from foraging to the use of ruminant livestock, to horse dairying and riding, and finally to the cultivation of grains. As part of my recently published book 'Domesticated', I propose a new model describing the stages of integration of cultivated species into societies. From the initial introduction of domesticated animals or plants to their acceptance, solidification or complete incorporation, and finally intensification. The delineation of these varied stages depends on refining broader narratives via novel biomolecular techniques including proteomics, ancient DNA, and isotopic analyses. Findings suggest that there were multiple trajectories and timelines for cooperation between species, as domesticates were integrated into societies. There were concurrent shifts in landscape use, knowledge systems, and the structures of social systems that encompassed cultivated species. While the spread of cultivated species occurred over varied landscapes and ecologies, the initial networks created formed the foundation for later iterations of the Silk Roads.
Alicia R. Ventresca-Miller is Associate Professor in the Department of Anthropology, Director of the Ancient Protein and Isotope Laboratory, and Associate Curator of Archaeological Sciences at the Museum of Anthropological Archaeology at the University of Michigan.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
Sandeep Sharma, Professor, CaltechNew Avenues in Cyclase Phase SynthesisInspired by the biosynthetic logic of terpene cyclase phase, we report a general strategy for the rapid and stereocontrolled construction of terpenoid architectures by overriding the inherent stereochemical outcome of polyolefin cyclizations. A central feature of this approach is a quaternary carbon center epimerization that precisely remodels the stereochemistry at one stereocenter, overcoming the conformational bias of the cyclization reaction. The key to our ketone epimerization is the design of a photoactive imine that circumvents the pitfalls of traditional carbonyl photochemistry. Visible-light excitation with a photosensitizer enables reversible C–C bond cleavage and reformation through a tertiary radical intermediate, thereby allowing epimerization of the adjacent quaternary center. We have recently applied this tactic toward the synthesis of several terpenoid natural products, including dasyscyphin A. This line of research is yielding protocols that reconfigure functionally inert stereocenters with unprecedented precision, unlocking new molecular skeletons and transformations long unattainable through existing methods.
The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: TDPS presents "Berkeley Dance Project: What Moves Between Us"
events.description: Choreography by SanSan Kwan (Two Doors) and Lisa Wymore (Cycle) Zellerbach Playhouse Showtimes: Thursday, February 18th at 8pm Friday, February 19th at 8pm Saturday, February 20th at 2pm Saturday, February 20th at 8pm Sunday, February 21st at 2pm Presented by the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies (TDPS) This collaboration offers two dance works that sit inside the friction of seeing and not seeing, doing and not doing. Together they unsettle passivity. They treat perception not as something fixed or solitary, but as something shared and in motion. The audience is invited not only to watch, but to notice and to sense where attention settles, and where it drifts. In this space, seeing, listening, and feeling become forms of participation. Two Doors is inspired by an incident in New York City in 2021 in which doormen closed their doors just afer seeing an attack on an Asian woman outside their lobby. Through a choreographic study of the aftermath of violence, Two Doors explores the viscerality of anti-Asian racism and the sovereignty that we wrest for ourselves in response. Dancers experiment with closings and openings, weight sharing and weight bearing, playing with the kinetics of in/visibility, and Asian American model minoritization. Two Doors depicts a journey toward self-possession via relational vulnerability. Cycle, inspired by Professor Georgina Kleege's book More Than Meets the Eye, is built with language and sound as equal partners with the dance. Audio description does not trail behind the movement - it generates it. The result is a reorientation of how we watch dance, and an insistence that dance can be heard, felt, and imagined beyond the primacy of sight.
