events.title: Manuel Trummer, "Raving Heritage: Berlin Techno between Underground and UNESCO"
events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room
events.description: In March 2024, the German Commission for UNESCO added Berlin's techno culture to the national inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage. For a music scene that emerged from the vacant spaces, squats, and legal grey zones of post-wall Berlin, official recognition is a complicated milestone. Professor Trummer will analyze why club collectives and activist networks deliberately pursued the UNESCO title and what happened once they got it. Rather than seeking state prestige, organizers mobilized the heritage campaign as an urban planning defense against commercial real estate pressures, soaring rents, and venue closures (Clubsterben). Yet reframing underground dance music as protected public heritage creates its own problems and new lines of conflict. Drawing on interviews with key scene actors, UNESCO policy debates, and a discourse analysis of the public media response to this unusual „cultural heritage", the talk examines the realities of this compromise. It asks whether intangible heritage status provides any real legal protection against eviction and noise complaints, or merely functions as cultural marketing for the city. It also looks at the internal tensions within the scene itself: how promoters, DJs, and ravers handle the contradiction between preserving an unruly, night-time counterculture and managing a state-sanctioned tradition. Finally, the case offers a broader perspective on the UNESCO framework today, pointing to how the heritage paradigm is shifting from regional crafts and rural folklore toward electronic, urban subcultures. Manuel Trummer is Professor and Chair of Empirical Cultural Studies and European Ethnology at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munich. Before that, he served as Managing Director of the Institute for Folklore Studies at the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities, taught at the University of Regensburg as an Associate Professor (Privatdozent), held a visiting fellowship at Leeds Beckett University, and was an extraordinary member of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences. Trained in European ethnology, folklore, and art history in Regensburg, where he earned both his doctorate and habilitation, Manuel Trummer explores how communities make sense of transformation across past and post-digital worlds. His work bridges vernacular narrative traditions—reflected in his role as co-editor of Fabula – Journal of Folktale Studies—with the politics of everyday culture, particularly in rural contexts. He currently directs two major, government-funded research projects investigating infrastructures and heritage practices across peripheral rural landscapes, and serves on the German Commission for UNESCO's Expert Committee on Intangible Cultural Heritage. His recent publications on these topics include "Listed! And Now What? Negotiating Uncertainty and Intangible Cultural Heritage in Rural Areas" (2025) and "The Rural as a Cultural Category" (Das Ländliche als kulturelle Kategorie, 2020). Alongside his work on folklore and space, he has written extensively on popular culture, rock music, and religion in mass media, including the co-edited volumes "Pop the Nation!" (2023) and "Sympathy for the Devil?" (2014). Outside this work, he spends his time with heavy guitar music and vintage folk horror.

events.title: 2027 Sheng Yen Conference
events.description:
The scholastic traditions associated with Sarvāstivāda and the Abhidharma corpus more broadly were transmitted to China beginning in the fourth and fifth centuries and became a significant focus of translation activity under the direction of Xuanzang in the seventh century. Yet modern scholarship often assumes that Chinese Buddhist scholiasts had little sustained interest in, or use for, Abhidharma. According to this view, Abhidharma was dismissed as "Hīnayāna" and overshadowed by the rise of indigenous Chinese Buddhist traditions such as Chan, Tiantai, and Huayan. There is, however, ample evidence that Abhidharma continued to be studied and valued by Chinese exegetes irrespective of their doctrinal or school affiliation, and that it retained an important place in monastic curricula from the medieval period down to the present day. This conference seeks to reconsider the reception and enduring influence of Abhidharma in Chinese Buddhism.

events.description: This talk explores a century-long tradition of anti-colonial Arab student activism on college campuses, one that crosses national boundaries, borders and liberation struggles. Beginning this story in the 1950s with the Organization of Arab Students of the U.S., Dr. Kehdi shows how students enactedArab Radical Literacies that respondedto the national liberation movements of their countries of origin, to U.S. Cold War policiesof containment, and to the imperial university's social engineering program of international student-exchange. events.title: Talk and Film Screening: Disavowal as Belonging
events.description:
This talk expands on Gelare Khoshgozaran's ongoing explorations of exile as a generative space to form a resonant collectivity—one that embodies alienation, embraces the impossibility of return, and makes a home through the continuous negotiation of borders. Three short films by the artist invite viewers to rethink cinema as a space to find our kin and comrades in exile spatially defined through the politics of belonging and disavowal.
Gelare Khoshgozaran is an undisciplinary artist and filmmaker whose work engages with legacies of imperial violence manifested in war, militarization, and borders. They use film and video to form narratives that seek to redefine existing constructions of 'home' as a means of conceptualizing other forms of belonging. Born and raised in a city of four seasons, they are an assistant professor of art at UCLA School of Art and Architecture.

events.title: Genentech Lecture
events.description: Huw Davies, Asa Griggs Candler Professor, Harvard UniversitySite-selective and enantioselective C–H functionalization controlled by induced fitting and secondary noncovalent interactions A major challenge in organic synthesis is the selective functionalization of C–H bonds. As most organic compounds contain multiple C–H bonds with similar properties, distinguishing between them requires precise control. For some time, we have been using high symmetry chiral dirhodium catalysts to control C-H functionalization with donor acceptor carbenes. In this presentation we will highlight the design of our most recent high symmetry dirhodium catalysts (C4 symmetric and D4 symmetric) and illustrate the subtle site-selectivity exhibited by these catalysts. We will show how they can adopt many of the characteristics atypically associated with enzymes, leading to unprecedented site-selectivity of nonactivated C–H bonds. The catalysts adopt a bowl-shape on formation and the flexible microenvironment within the bowl causes an induced fitting to occur as the reagent and the substrate approach the catalyst. Recent synthetic application of this methodology to the synthesis of various chiral scaffolds will be described.

events.title: The Lost Fairy Tales of the Brothers Grimm
events.description: A lecture on Franz Xaver von Schönwerth (1810-1886), one of the most prominent disciples of the Brothers Grimm, yet still largely unknown outside Germany. When The Guardian and The Washington Post in 2015 reported on the rediscovery of a historical folktale collection from Bavaria, both outlets called it "the lost fairy tales of the Brothers Grimm." The material was actually collected by Franz Xaver von Schönwerth (1810–1886), a Bavarian civil servant whom Jacob Grimm praised as the only scholar capable of continuing his and Wilhelm's work. Outside Germany, however, Schönwerth was largely forgotten. This talk introduces Schnwerth in the context of nineteenth-century German folklore studies (Volkskunde). Like Jacob Grimm, Schönwerth worked within the mythological school of Romanticism, convinced that rural folklore, dialect, and customs preserved remnants of an ancient Germanic past. At the same time, his fieldwork was unusually rigorous for its era. Instead of rewriting stories for middle-class readers as the Grimms did, Schönwerth took down local narratives in the Upper Palatinate with strict attention to dialect, raw phrasing, and local variants. The presentation examines how Schönwerth combined Romantic nationalist assumptions about myth with systematic ethnographic documentation. Finally, it turns to his reception today, looking at the vibrant "afterlife" of Schönwerth, and how regional initiatives, online media, and popular adaptations have turned a nineteenth-century field collection into new digital folklore.

events.title: Vienna Philharmonic
events.description: Tuesday, March 2, 7:30pm Wednesday, March 3, 7:30pmThursday, March 4, 7pmOrchestraThe Maria Manetti Shrem and Elizabeth SegerstromCalifornia Orchestra ResidencyVienna PhilharmonicYannick Nézet-Séguin, conductor Program:Tuesday, March 2, 7:30pmVienna PhilharmonicYannick Nézet-Séguin, conductor Mahler/Symphony No. 9 Wednesday, March 3, 7:30pmVienna PhilharmonicYannick Nézet-Sguin, conductorYuja Wang, pianoChristiane Karg, soprano Prokofiev/Piano Concerto No. 3 Mahler/Symphony No. 4 Thursday, March 4, 7pmVienna PhilharmonicYannick Nézet-Séguin, conductorChristiane Karg, sopranoElīna Garanča, mezzo-sopranoSan Francisco Symphony ChorusJenny Wong, director Mahler/Symphony No. 2, Resurrection The Vienna Philharmonic returns to Berkeley for three concerts led by maestro Yannick Nézet-Séguin in the 2027 The Maria Manetti Shrem and Elizabeth Segerstrom California Orchestra Residency. The revered 185-year-old orchestra and star conductor have enjoyed a close partnership over many years, a relationship finely honed through numerous tours and recordings. For these performances the focus is Mahler, a particularly important figure in the Philharmonic's history whose Ninth Symphony received its posthumous premiere by the orchestra in 1912. The composer's music is a perfect match for the towering institution, which will be joined by a selection of internationally acclaimed guest artists throughout the Berkeley residency. The first performance features Mahler's poignant final completed symphony, one of the most profound and emotionally complex works in the orchestral repertoire. The second night features both Mahler's Fourth Symphony, with Christiane Karg as soprano soloist, and Prokofiev's Concerto in C major, with superstar pianist Yuja Wang joining at the keyboard. In the final program, Mahler's Resurrection symphony takes the listener on a journey through earthly trials to ultimate transcendence, and features vocalists Christiane Karg and Elīna Garanča, and the San Francisco Symphony Chorus. events.title: An Evening with Arthur Sze
events.location: Heyns Room, The Faculty Club, UC Berkeley
events.description:
RSVP (https://lp.constantcontactpages.com/ev/reg/vn6x27c) is required.
Arthur Sze is a poet, translator, and editor, and in 2025 he was named the 25th Poet Laureate of the United States. He is the author of twelve books of poetry, including Into the Hush (2025) and The White Orchard: Selected Interviews, Essays, and Poems (2025); The Glass Constellation: New and Collected Poems (2021); Sight Lines (2019), for which he won the National Book Award; Compass Rose (2014); The Ginkgo Light (2009); Quipu (2005); The Redshifting Web: Poems 1970–1998 (1998); and Archipelago (1995). He also authored Transient Worlds: On Translating Poetry (forthcoming from Copper Canyon Press, 2026), The Silk Dragon II: Translations of Chinese Poetry (2024), and edited Chinese Writers on Writing (2010). His poetry has been translated into fifteen languages, including Chinese, Dutch, German, Portuguese, and Spanish. Sze received the 2025 Bollingen Prize for lifetime achievement in American poetry, the 2024 Rebekah Johnson Bobbitt National Prize for Poetry, 2024 National Book Foundation Science + Literature award, the Ruth Lilly Poetry Prize, the Shelley Memorial Award, the Jackson Poetry Prize, a Lannan Literary Award, and a Guggenheim Fellowship, among others. A chancellor emeritus of the Academy of American Poets and a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, he was the 2023–2024 Mohr Visiting Poet at Stanford University. Professor emeritus at the Institute of American Indian Arts (IAIA), Sze was the first poet laureate of Santa Fe, where he lives with his wife, the poet Carol Moldaw. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Department of English.

Jonathan Kief (https://asianstudies.unc.edu/faculty/kief-i-jonathan/) (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill).Triangle Republics is a groundbreaking contribution to literary studies of Korea and beyond, one that turns the production and circulation of texts into the occasion for rethinking the impact of the Cold War on the Korean peninsula and its diaspora. Upending the conventional view of the Korean division as one of separation and antagonism between two diametrically opposed and mutually exclusive cultural spheres, the book reveals how North and South Korean literature surreptitiously formed and transformed each other through the Korean diaspora in Japan. Following the circuit of Korean texts via Japan from 1945 until the 1980s, Kief uncovers the creative ways that writers, critics, and intellectuals crossed the boundaries of nation, language, ideology, and genre to challenge Cold War entrenchments. This required tracking not only Korean language texts, but also Japanese language ones, often published in obscure journals, painstakingly gathered from multiple archives through rigorous research employing cross-disciplinary tools and methods. The result is a work that changes not only what we know about Cold War Korean literature, but also how we might write cultural and intellectual history when the nation-state is no longer assumed to be its natural container. Established in 2022 to honor Berkeley Political Science Professor and longtime CKS Chair Hong Yung Lee (1939-2017), each year this award and its $10,000 prize recognizes a groundbreaking, English-language academic monograph that advances Korean Studies by combining scholarly merit, research prowess, and methodological innovation. The award recognizes Professor Lee's enduring influence on Korean Studies, but also commitment to situating the field in a broad intellectual landscape. Learn more about the Hong Yung Lee Book Award here: https://ieas.berkeley.edu/cks/hylbookaward (https://ieas.berkeley.edu/cks/hylbookaward) Triangle Republics is available for purchase in paperback, hard copy, and as an e-book. You can order copies of the book in all formats here:https://cup.columbia.edu/book/triangle-republics/9780231219846/ (https://cup.columbia.edu/book/triangle-republics/9780231219846/) Awardee Bio: I. Jonathan Kief is Associate Professor of Korean Studies at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where he also serves as Associate Chair and Director of Graduate Studies in the Department of Asian and Middle Eastern Studies. He is a scholar of modern Korean literature and culture whose research explores the movement of words, sounds, and ideas across the spatial, ideological, and media boundaries of the Cold War era. His first book, Triangle Republics: Cross-Border Literary Transits between the Cold War Koreas and Japan (Columbia UP, 2025), follows the multi-directional itineraries of literary exchange linking Cold War-era North Korea, South Korea, and Japan. His second book, tentatively titled "Interference/Interface: Broadcast Sound in the Divided Koreas," looks at how wired and wireless broadcasts crossed the Cold War Koreas, reshuffled media and genre boundaries, and transformed conceptions of labor, leisure, gender, and power.

events.title: Shiben Banerji | Object, Site, Antecedent, Exemplar: India in the Occult Imagination of the Globe
events.description:
A talk by Shiben Banerji, (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/shiben-banerji) Associate Professor of Architecture and Urbanism, History of Art Department, at UC Berkeley, exploring how occult and modernist visions of global unity drew on colonial India to shape early twentieth-century debates on architecture, urban planning, and a shared global ethos.
Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley will serve as discussant.
Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ——–DATE: Thu, Mar 4, 2027 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————- ABSTRACT The wars, rebellions, revolutions, and slumps of the early twentieth century seemed destined to rip asunder the ties that bound colonizers and colonized subjects to one another. The upheaval represented an opportunity, and not just for nationalists who imagined new homelands or for socialists who dreamed of international brotherhood. For modernists in the orbit of various occultisms, the crisis of empire also represented an opportunity to reveal humanity's fundamental unity and common fate. In this talk, Shiben Banerji critiques representations of India in occult imaginings of a global future for metropolitan and colonized societies. Focusing on prints, drawings, buildings, and films, as well as on texts in Dutch, French, Italian, Spanish, German, English, Hindi, Gujarati, and Bengali, created between 1905 and 1945 across the Americas, Europe, South Asia, and Australia, the talk reconstructs the centrality of late colonial India and early post-independence India in early twentieth-century debates on the virtue of forming a global ethos in planned urban space. SPEAKER BIOShiben Banerji (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/shiben-banerji) is Associate Professor in the Dept of History of Art. He interested in the rhetorical and performative dimensions of architecture. His classroom teaching and historical scholarship are animated by three questions. First, how did architects in early modern Europe describe their interest in the nature of political oratory at the very moment that they began studying architectural forms that were not derived from Roman antiquity? Second, how did architects across the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia mediate new conceptions of public association in the context of nineteenth-century colonialisms, and how did concomitant experiments in old and new media present architectural and urban space as objects of artistic depiction and literary invention? Third, how did twentieth-century theorists of alternatives to liberal modernity in the ex-colonial world conceptualize the work of architectural media in altering perception and consciousness? Shiben is the author of Lineages of the Global City(link is external) (University of Texas Press, 2025), which was supported by a Mellon fellowship in the urban humanities and a publication grant from the Graham Foundation. Explicating the conjunction of planning and occultism in the early twentieth century, the book examines the designation of planned urban space as a site for forming a global ethos—meaning both an outlook on oneself as inescapably linked to every creature and thing, as well as the obligation to choose and act with a regard for one's inexorable impact on others. A similar attention to forms of rhetorical action that sustain notions of belonging informs Shiben's coedited volume In the Shadows of Democracy(link is external) (Intermezzo, 2025). Shiben is currently writing Time on the Road to Civil Rights, which foregrounds the salience of planning in civil rights discourse to advance a genealogical critique of the synchronic emergence of rhetorical theory and planning theory in the mid-twentieth century. He has also begun editing an anthology of uses and meanings of "spirit" in twentieth-century aesthetic, economic, and political thought. A dedicated teacher, Shiben was named Faculty of the Year by his students at the School of Art of Institute of Chicago when he was an Assistant Professor. To encourage new lines of graduate research, Shiben regularly contributes to Oxford Bibliographies in Architecture, Planning, and Preservation. ______ The South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/saai) at the University of California, Berkeley promotes research-based conversations and collaborations around the arts of South Asia + its diasporas from the ancient period to the now. To read more about the Initiative and help support its various fundraising goals, please click HERE (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/saai) ______ Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: TDPS presents "Melancholy Play" by Sarah Ruhl
events.description: by Sarah Ruhl Directed by Patrick Russell Durham Studio Theater Showtimes: Thursday, March 11th at 8pm Friday, March 12th at 8pm Saturday, March 13th at 2pm Saturday, March 13th at 8pm Sunday, March 14th at 2pm Presented by the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies (TDPS) What if sadness were an exquisite force of beauty? For Tilly, a melancholic bank teller, her heaviness becomes something luminous—strangely alluring, powerfully magnetic—drawing others toward her with a disarming pull and, in the process, revealing their truest selves. The poetic farce of Melancholy Play invites us into a whimsical world where emotional truth is contagious, where identities slip free from the mundanity of everyday life and reform in response to longing, perception, and desire. Moving between sincerity and absurdity, Tilly's journey creates a space where vulnerability and humor coexist, and where transformation becomes both surprising and inevitable, unfolding in a world that is at once heightened and immediate. This surreal, magical story speaks to the simple truths of the human condition: the need for connection, and the profound value of feeling deeply. events.title: A Book of the Civic Silk Road: Translating Ming China for the Ottoman World
events.description:
A Book of the Civic Silk Road: Translating Ming China for the Ottoman World The Book of China is the most detailed description of China's government and society written by any foreigner before the age of European maritime empires. 'Ali Akbar Khatayi, a Persian-speaking merchant from Central Eurasia, spent six years in China around 1503 before traveling west to Ottoman Istanbul where he completed his book in 1516. Khatayi description of the Ming state advances a theory of bureaucracy that anticipates that of Max Weber. His vivid descriptions of Ming society range in content from the lunar New Year to funerary customs to street toughs and legends of flying monks. Drawing on our new annotated English translation, we explore how knowledge of Ming China was transmitted across the Persianate and Ottoman intellectual worlds, while also examining his account alongside contemporary Chinese sources.
Kaveh L. Hemmat is Associate Professor of History at Benedictine University. His research focuses on interaction between the Islamic world and East Asia with a focus on representations of East Asia in Islamicate political writing. He is also translator of the Kushnameh: The Persian Epic of Kush the Tusked, and co-editor and translator of the Book of China.
Hyunhee Park is Professor of History at the City University of New York, John Jay College of Criminal Justice and the CUNY Graduate Center. She specializes in cross-cultural exchanges in premodern Eurasia, particularly between the Islamic world and East Asia, author of Mapping the Chinese and Islamic Worlds and Soju: A Global History, and co-editor of the Book of China.

events.location: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, 2334 Bowditch Street
events.description:
Event description Is vote buying effective? Kenneth Greene will discuss his new book, Againstthe Machine: Why Party Competition Disrupts Vote Buying (Cambridge University Press, 2026), which offers a novel theory about the conditions that make vote-buying attempts succeed or fail. Politicians in at least 73 countries around the world engage in systematic vote-buying schemes. Perhaps surprisingly, offering cash, food, clothing, building materials, access to medical services, legal aid, and other benefits rarely wins new votes. Contrasting with the grim implications of the long-held assumption that vote buying is always effective, Greene's argument yields an optimistic take on elections, the voting behavior of poor citizens, and the potential for political representation in new democracies.
SpeakerKenneth Greene (https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.kenneth-greene.com/&source=gmail-imap&ust=1790021376000000&usg=AOvVaw21GrQ4bIufKtKJ7J_dYRtL) is Professor of Government at the University of Texas at Austin where he studies democratization and political behavior in new democracies, including vote buying and political polarization. His research has won a best book award and five best paper awards from the American Political Science Association.
Organized by Professor Alison Post, co-sponsored by CLACS and the Department of Political Science.

The Later Spread Spreading Further: Study of A Tangut Tantric Anthology
events.description:
The Later Spread Spreading Further: Study of A Tangut Tantric AnthologyLeong Clancy Fellowship Annual Lecture 2026 The past two decades have seen a steady growth in scholarship on the influences of Tibetan Buddhism in the Tangut State, also known as Xixia (Chin. 西夏) or Minyak (Tib. མི་ཉག་/མེ་ཉག་). During the period of its sovereignty between the 11th and the 13th century, this inner Asian state actively promoted various Tibetan Buddhist traditions, as attested by the abundant Tibetan Buddhist materials in multiple languages unearthed from important archaeological sites. While they enjoyed popularity and authority in the Tangut State, these traditions were themselves the products of a highly eclectic era in Tibet, the so-called "Later Spread of Buddhism" (Tib. bstan pa phyi dar), when Tibetan intellectuals were assimilating the newly imported Indic teachings. This talk focuses on a Tangut manuscript that presents an anthology of five tantric Buddhist texts. While the contents reflect a known tantric practice lineage from twelfth-century Tibet with some Tibetan textual counterparts already identified, this talk will examine some textual discrepancies between the Tangut and Tibetan versions. These discrepancies, along with the Tangut texts' anthologized format, lead to the conclusion that they might not be literal translations of the Tibetan counterparts. Instead, I propose that the anthology might have served the pragmatic purposes of local interests in the tantric rituals. Then too, the talk demonstrates how these Tibetan Buddhist materials from the Tangut State may be used to enrich our knowledge of the "Later Spread", a formative era in the history of Tibetan Buddhism.
Xingjian Zhang is a PhD student in the Group in Buddhist Studies at UC Berkeley. He received a B.A. in World History and Foreign Languages (Archaeology track) from Peking University in 2022 and an M.A. in Religion and Philosophy in Asia from LMU Munich in 2025. He is primarily interested in the history and literature of Tibetan Buddhist traditions in the 11th–13th centuries, with a particular focus on their transmission into the Tangut State (Xixia).

events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room
events.description: From Indo-Portuguese to Goan: the Role of Folk Expressions in Architecture In recent decades, scholarship on the Portuguese legacy in artistic expressions in Asia has hesitated to move beyond the global taxonomy of Indo-Portuguese, especially because of the difficulties of choosing or assuming the obvious terms on a case-by-case basis. Nationalisms, in the context of the nation-state crisis and religious-ethnic conflicts, are key clues to explaining this hesitation. Goan Catholic architecture is omnipresent in the promotional material of that fast-developing Indian state, an indisputable emblem of its brand and identity. What has defined its distinctive expression, its architectural grammar and discourse? In this lecture, I will present my contribution: between the colonial and the Goan, folk played a decisive role. Walter Rossa (Caracas, 1962), Architect (Lisbon, 1985), MA in History of Art (Lisbon, 1991), PhD and aggregated in Architecture (Coimbra, 2001 and 2013). Professor in the Department of Architecture and researcher at the Centre for the History of Society and Culture of the University of Coimbra. He holds the UNESCO Chair in Intercultural Dialogue in Heritages of Portuguese Influence (2019) and teaches courses in cultural heritage, town and regional planning, urban design, history, and architecture. Beyond his past work as a practising architect and town planner, he dedicated his efforts last year to cooperation and the relationship among heritage, history, planning, and development. He seeks to establish links between his academic work and development cooperation activities. A significant set of his publications is available at https://coimbra.academia.edu/WalterRossa

Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
Anna Wuttig, Neubauer Family Assistant Professor, University of ChicagoDesigning for Disorder: Electrocatalytic Synthesis with Interfacial Control Chemical synthesis driven by electricity offers a sustainable, scalable, decentralized, and energy-efficient route to furnish value-added products – from fuels to complex molecules. Maximizing reaction efficiency and durability requires immobilized catalytic active sites on electrodes, resulting in dispersed and non-uniform sites. This heterogeneity challenges iterative optimization of reactivity through traditional catalyst modifications, which rely on uniform, singular active sites. How do we rationally enhance electrocatalysis if the active sites cannot be identified or found? This lecture focuses on my group's catalyst development strategy designed for this disorder, enabling efficient and selective chemical synthesis by heterogenous electrocatalysts. First, we have developed a non-covalent synthetic strategy for tuning charge transfer at electrodes with molecularly tunable, regenerative, and recoverable surface layers prepared in a single, in-situ step. Applicable to various electrode materials and morphologies, thus compatible with disordered active sites, these layers enable enhanced durability and cyclability of catalytic energy conversion systems and enable order-of-magnitude enhancements in the rates of hydrogen peroxide production. Second, we have advanced the use of reusable catalytic electrodes, with their interfacial structure tuned by the addition of Lewis and Brønsted acids, for reductive fragment-based electrophile coupling to forge C(sp3)-C(sp3) bonds and the preparation of derivatized bioactive compounds. Our methods development is guided by in-situ spectroscopies, revealing the substrate- and intermediate-electrode interactions that redirect product selectivity. Combining these advances with mechanistic studies and electrochemical modelling, we introduce a conceptual catalyst development framework where the inherent structural disorder of heterogeneous electrocatalysts systems is a feature, not a deterrent.

events.title: Lecture: Aurélie Godet, "The Festive Work of Empire: Ritual and Colonial Power in French Louisiana"
events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room
events.description:
How did the French monarchy govern a distant and precarious colony such as Louisiana? This lecture by Aurélie Godet (Nantes) argues that ceremony and festivity constituted a "technology" of imperial power as much as military force, administrative regulation, and Catholic evangelization. Royal celebrations, religious processions, Te Deum services, and other officially sanctioned festivities were transferred from metropolitan France to Louisiana as part of an imperial cultural policy designed to reproduce the ceremonial idiom of the monarchy overseas. Yet these rituals were not simply transplanted: colonial governors adapted and sometimes instrumentalized them to cultivate the allegiance of local elites, while their capacity to generate collective joy helped naturalize social and political hierarchies. For the Indigenous and African populations who inhabited this imperial festive landscape, festivity could function as a form of "counter-technology." Indigenous ceremonial practices – including calumet rituals, gift-giving, feasting, music, and dance – did not merely facilitate French diplomacy but enabled Native communities to reshape and sometimes contest the ritual terms of imperial encounters. Likewise, enslaved Africans exploited the temporal and spatial openings created by the colonial religious calendar and the ambiguities of the 1724 slave code to organize feasts and "noces." Such gatherings helped preserve cultural practices, create alternative communities, and occasionally challenge colonial restrictions on mobility and interracial sociability. By examining festivity as both an instrument and a site of contestation, this talk proposes to broaden the concept of imperial technology beyond bureaucratic and material systems to include the management of collective affect.
Aurélie Godet is Professor of North American History at Nantes Université, France, and a junior fellow of the Institut Universitaire de France (2023–2028). After a decade of research on the history and ascendency of conservative movements and ideas in the United States, she shifted her focus in 2015 to the history of festivity in the Americas, with particular attention to the circulation of festive practices in the Atlantic world from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century. She recently completed a manuscript entitled Empire of Joy? The Cultural Politics of Festivity in French Colonial Louisiana (1682-1769), and serves on the editorial board of the Journal of Festive Studies, the peer-reviewed online journal she cofounded in 2019.

Jeff Bandar, Associate Professor, Colorado State UniversityNew Concepts in Acid-Base Chemistry and Their Synthetic ApplicationsOur group's overarching goal is to establish new acid-base reactivity principles as a means to advance synthetic chemistry. For example, while base-promoted reactions typically accomplish redox neutral transformations, such as the addition of pronucleophiles to electrophiles, we have identified general strategies for base-promoted oxidative and reductive coupling reactions. This talk will discuss the development of these strategies for a diverse range of new C–H bond functionalization reactions. The mechanistic frameworks of these methods will be compared to traditional base-promoted protocols to demonstrate unique capabilities and broad synthetic potential. To conclude, new perspectives of fundamental acid-base paradigms that are inspired by this work will be shown as the foundation for our group's future directions.

events.title: Ayesha S. ​Mahmud | Infectious Diseases in an Era of Global Change: Examples from Bangladesh
events.description:
A talk by Ayesha S. ​Mahmud (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/ayesha-mahmud), Associate Professor of Demography, UC Berkeley on the demographic and climatic drivers of infectious diseases in Bangladesh, with broader implications for the future burden of infectious diseases globally.
Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, April 13, 2027 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) —————- ABSTRACT The ecological landscape of our planet is increasingly being shaped by a combination of global demographic shifts, such as rapid urbanization and increased human connectivity, and climatic changes, such as increases in mean temperatures and a greater frequency of extreme weather events. These global changes have important consequences for the emergence, evolution, geographic spread, and burden of infectious diseases. This talk will present insights from recent work on the demographic and climatic drivers of infectious diseases in Bangladesh, with broader implications for the future burden of infectious diseases globally. SPEAKER BIOAyesha S. ​Mahmud (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/ayesha-mahmud) is an Associate Professor of Demography at UC Berkeley. Her research broadly examines the interplay between population change, environmental factors, and infectious disease dynamics. Drawing on theory and methods from demography and disease ecology, her work explores questions such as why outbreaks occur at particular times of year, how and why the mortality burden of infectious diseases changes over time, how population mobility shapes the spatial dynamics of outbreaks, and how global environmental and demographic change may alter patterns of infectious disease burden in the future. She uses statistical methods and biologically mechanistic models to investigate these questions across a range of diseases and settings in Asia, Africa, and Central America, drawing on data from disease surveillance systems, hospital databases, climate models, human mobility data, and population surveys and censuses. Prior to joining UC Berkeley, Mahmud was a Rockefeller Foundation Planetary Health Fellow at Harvard University. She received her PhD in Demography from Princeton University in 2017.

The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. _____________ Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Ning Zheng: Molecular Glues: From Mechanisms to Therapeutics
events.description:
Molecular glue (MG) degraders represent an exciting new modality in drug discovery highlighted by their ability to degrade undruggable targets and their favorable pharmacological properties. Thus far, only a very small number of MG degraders have been serendipitously found, most of which act on CULLIN4 E3 ubiquitin ligases. The scarcity of these novel compounds limits our understanding of their activity requirement, E3 ligases preference, and functional versatility, thereby hindering the prospective discovery of new MG degraders. In this presentation, I will highlight our latest studies on the identification of new MG degrader compounds as well as human disease mutations acting as genetic glues that foster neo-substrate-E3 interactions. These findings point to potential rational strategy for rational discovery of target-centric MG degraders.
Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: (Thomas Carell) Cynthia A. Chan Memorial Lecture: "The second dimension of the genetic code"
events.description: Cynthia A. Chan Memorial Lecture - DNA stores genetic information in the sequence of the four canonical bases dA, dC, dG, and T and, in addition, carries epigenetic information encoded by the four modified cytidine bases: 5-methylcytidine (mdC), 5-hydroxymethylcytidine (hmdC), 5-formylcytidine (fdC), and 5-carboxycytidine (cadC), with 5-hydroxymethyluridine (hmdU) potentially playing a role as well. These additional nucleosides are generated by TET(1–3) enzymes, which catalyze the stepwise oxidation of mdC or T to all the others, with the help of oxygen and -ketoglutarate. This oxidation chemistry in the genome thus establishes a second, largely uncharted layer of information. While the sequence code is static, the writing and erasure of the epigenetic code creates a dynamic information layer that controls gene activity, e.g. the differentiation of cells or memory formation and erasure in the brain. In this lecture, I will cover the discovery of the new epigenetic bases that expand the genetic alphabet using quantitative mass spectrometry and I will discuss new insights into their symmetry and localization based on recent sequencing data. I will then describe how the TET-based chemistry is now being exploited to develop new epigenetic sequencing methods that enable earlier cancer detection, thereby improving the chances of successful treatment. If time permits, I will also discuss why the modified base pseudouridine in mRNA allows the molecule to evade the innate immune system.

events.title: Le Concert des Nations; Jordi Savall, director: Beethoven Symphonies Nos. 3 & 5
events.description: Friday, April 23, 7:30pm OrchestraLe Concert des NationsJordi Savall, directorBeethoven Symphonies Nos. 3 & 5 Program: Beethoven/Symphony No. 3, Eroica Symphony No. 5 In Jordi Savall's programs, Berkeley audiences have come to expect the unexpected and painstakingly curated works by lesser-known and often anonymous composers that explore history and reveal connections between people and cultures. Sunday, April 25, 3pmEarly Music: Opera & OratorioThe English ConcertHandel'sAlessandroHarry Bicket, conductor and harpsichord Christophe Dumaux,countertenor (Alessandro)
Joélle Harvey, soprano (Lisaura)

Ashley Riches,baritone (Clito)
Alexander Chance,countertenor (Cleone)
Anthony Gregory,tenor (Leonato) Program: The musicians of The English Concert return for their annual Berkeley engagement with a concert presentation of Handel's 1726 opera Alessandro. The lively, charming score explores the romantic life of conqueror Alexander the Great, focusing less on Alessandro's acts of war and more on his turbulent love triangle with the two women who vie for his affection. French countertenor and Handel specialist Christophe Dumaux is Alessandro; American soprano Joélle Harvey plays Lisaura, and Australian mezzo-soprano Xenia Puskarz Thomas is her competitor, Rossane. events.title: TDPS presents "Indeed, friend!" by Eliza Bent
events.description: By Eliza Bent Directed by Nancy Carlin Zellerbach Playhouse Showtimes: Thursday, April 29th at 8pm Friday, April 30th at 8pm Saturday, May 1st at 2pm Saturday, May 1st at 8pm Sunday, May 2nd at 2pm Presented by the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies (TDPS) Indeed, friend! by Eliza Bent explores a group of undergrad college students, on the editorial board of a student published arts and literature magazine, who meet regularly in a basement office over the course of the 2000-2001 academic year. We watch these misfit students work together, as they hunger for meaning, amusement, validation and relationship. How does creativity help shape what kind of adult we become? How do we best adjudicate a piece of art? A life? The production, which will be performed on a stage shared with the audience, in the Zellerbach Playhouse, invites the audience to feel included in these monthly editorial meetings. events.title: Lecture: The Afterlives of Resource Sovereignty
events.description:
According to a 1959 issue of the Middle East Economic Digest, nearly sixty percent of the global reserves in oil were held by five US-based companies (three of which were descendants of Standard Oil), another eighteen percent by two British firms (Shell and British Petroleum), and the remainder by the Soviet Union, Mexico and other, smaller, producers. Thirty years later, and after the tumultuous struggle for resource sovereignty, nationalisation of oil had enacted what historian Christopher Dietrich has called "the most concentrated peacetime transfer of wealth in history." In this talk, Dr Laleh Khalili will advance a provisional argument about how states, corporations, and capitalists that formerly benefited from their ownership of oil recuperated from such massive losses by their transformation of the mechanisms for pricing oil, exploring for and exploiting it, accounting for it, financing it, and transporting it. These new mechanisms were directly responsible for the dismantling of social democracy in the global North and the moment of decolonization in the global South.
Laleh Khalili is a professor of Gulf Studies at the University of Exeter, and the author or editor of seven books including most recently Sinews of War and Trade: Shipping and Capitalism in the Arabian Peninsula (Verso 2020) and Extractive Capitalism: How Commodities and Cronyism Drive the Global Economy (Profile 2025).

events.title: Workshop: Work, War and Commerce
events.location: Center for Middle Eastern Studies, 340 Stephens Hall
events.description: In this workshop, we will read about the intertwined lives of war and commerce, and the people who work and whose work is defined by them. The workshop will engage with theoretical as well as empirical research works that engage with the work of trade, communication and transportation and the central role violence plays in their working and asks how do we research these intertwined subjects? About the Instructor:Laleh Khalili (https://experts.exeter.ac.uk/41005-laleh-khalili) is a professor of Gulf Studies at the University of Exeter, and the author or editor of seven books including most recently Sinews of War and Trade: Shipping and Capitalism in the Arabian Peninsula (Verso 2020) and Extractive Capitalism: How Commodities and Cronyism Drive the Global Economy (Profile 2025). On Thursday, April 29th, Dr. Khalili will be delivering lecture The Afterlives of Resource Sovereignty in Maude Fife Room on UC Berkeley's campus. Click here (https://iranianstudies.berkeley.edu/lecture-afterlives-resource-sovereignty) to learn more about the event.

events.title: Lunch Poems: Beth Piatote
events.description: Lunch Poems (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/lunch-poems), Berkeley's storied noontime poetry series, welcomes Beth Piatote. Beth Piatote is a Nez Perce writer, scholar, and playwright and an associate professor of English and comparative literature at UC Berkeley. She specializes in interdisciplinary approaches to Native American literature; creative writing; Nez Perce language and literature; and Indigenous language revitalization more broadly. Piatote is the author of three books and two plays. Her most recent publication is distant water: poems, from Milkweed Editions in 2026. The collection explores the way Nez Perce language embodies the inseparable connection of land, sound, and spirit. Her poems, scholarly essays, and short stories have appeared in Poetry, World Literature Today, PMLA, The Kenyon Review, The Stinging Fly, and elsewhere. The Lunch Poems series, founded by Professor Robert Hass, is supported by Dr. and Mrs. Tom Colby, the UC Berkeley Library, the Morrison Library Fund, the UC Berkeley English Department, and the Deans' Office of the College of Letters & Science. For more information or to be added to the Lunch Poems mailing list, please email poems-library@berkeley.edu (mailto:poems-library@berkeley.edu) or follow @PoemsLunch on Instagram (http://instagram.com/poemslunch) and X (https://twitter.com/PoemsLunch).

events.title: Book Talk: Chop Fry Watch Learn: Fu-Pei Mei and the Making of Modern Chinese Food | Lecture by Michelle King
events.description:
Fu Pei-mei (1931-2004), Taiwan's beloved and pioneering postwar cook book author and television celebrity, was often called the "Julia Child of Chinese cooking." Fu appeared continuously on television for forty years, wrote dozens of best-selling Chinese cookbooks, owned a successful cooking school and traveled the world, teaching foreigners about Chinese food. Women in her generation, which included both housewives and career women, turned to Fu because she taught them how to cook an astounding range of unfamiliar Chinese regional dishes, in ways their own mothers and grandmothers never could. Her cookbook also represents the transpacific journeys of thousands of migrants, as they carried her recipes in their suitcases, traveling far from home. Fu's story offers us a window onto not just food, but also family, gender roles, technology, media, foreign relations, and cultural identity. This is not just a story of timeless culinary tradition, but one of modern transformation– of self and family, of cuisine and society. This talk will focus on Fu's bilingual cookbooks and her appeal to audiences in Taiwan, the United States, and around the world. Speaker Bio:Michelle T. King, professor of history at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, specializes in modern Chinese food and gender history. She is the author of Chop Fry Watch Learn: Fu Pei-mei and the Making of Modern Chinese Food (W. W. Norton, 2024), which was named a notable book of 2024 by the New York Times, NPR, and Saveur, and shortlisted for the Baifang Schell China Book Prize.
She is also co-editor of Modern Chinese Foodways (MIT Press, 2025), editor of Culinary Nationalism in Asia (Bloomsbury Academic, 2019), and the recipient of fellowships from the NEH and ALCS.
